docs.title: Background jobs and scheduled tasks in Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to move slow work out of the request with a queue, and how to run work on a timer with the scheduler.

Some work is too slow for a request. Sending an email can take a second or more. A report can take a minute. The user should not wait for it.

Some work has no request at all. A daily summary email, or a cleanup of old rows at night.

Dox has two packages for this:

  • dox_queue runs jobs in the background. It has retries, delays and a worker process.
  • dox_scheduler runs tasks on a schedule, like cron, written in Dart.

The example is a team app with projects and tasks. It sends a welcome email when a user signs up, a daily summary of open tasks, and it cleans up old data at night.

docs.title: The steps in short
docs.text:
1. Pick a queue driver. A new app already has the queue and the scheduler.
  2. Add dox_mailer to send email.
  3. Queue the welcome email with one line.
  4. Write a job for the daily summary.
  5. Put the job and a cleanup task on the schedule.
  6. Run the worker and the scheduler next to the server.
  7. Test it with no real queue.

docs.title: 1. The queue
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has dox_queue and dox_scheduler, with these files:

  • lib/config/queue.dart and lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
  • lib/config/schedule.dart and lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart
  • bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart

The queue uses the database driver by default. Make its tables once:

dox queue:table
dox migrate
lib/config/queue.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../generated/jobs.g.dart';

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  /// sync, database or redis
  driver: 'database',

  /// every @Job class, from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart
  jobs: jobRegistry,
);

The database driver needs nothing more than the database you already have. For many jobs, switch to redis.

docs.title: 2. Add mail
docs.text:
dart pub add dox_mailer
lib/config/mail.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'Team app'),
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing. Good for local work.
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);
lib/providers/mail_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}

SMTP, Amazon SES, Resend, Mailgun and Postmark all work. You change the provider in the config, not in the code.

docs.title: 3. Queue the welcome email
docs.text:
A mailable is one kind of email in its own class:

dox make:mail Welcome
lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart
class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email!, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome to the team';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}

Now send it from the queue, after sign up:

lib/app/services/user.service.dart
Future<User> signUp(SignUp body) async {
  User user = await users.create(body);
  await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
  return user;
}

queue() renders the email at once and puts it on the queue. The request answers right away. A worker sends the email. You need no job class for this. dox_mailer has a built-in job for email.

docs.title: 4. Write a job
docs.text:
For your own work, write a job class. The daily summary loads the open tasks of a user and emails them:

dox make:job SendDailySummary
lib/app/jobs/send_daily_summary.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

@Job()
class SendDailySummary extends DoxJob {
  SendDailySummary({required this.userId});

  final int userId;

  /// run up to 3 times
  @override
  int get tries => 3;

  /// wait 1 minute before the 2nd try, 5 minutes before the 3rd
  @override
  List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[
    Duration(minutes: 1),
    Duration(minutes: 5),
  ];

  @override
  String get queue => 'emails';

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    SummaryService summary = Dox().ioc.get<SummaryService>();
    await summary.sendTo(userId);
  }

  /// runs once, after the last try failed
  @override
  Future<void> failed(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
    Logger.warn('daily summary of user $userId failed: $error');
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job. It writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart, so the worker knows how to save and load the job.

Two rules for jobs:

  • Save an id, not an object. The job saves userId, not a User. The user can change between dispatch and run. The id gives fresh data.
  • Get services in handle(). A job is made again from its saved data, so it can not get services in its constructor. Use Dox().ioc.get<T>().

Dispatch it from anywhere:

await SendDailySummary(userId: user.id!).dispatch();

// later, or at a time
await SendDailySummary(userId: 1).dispatch(delay: Duration(minutes: 10));

docs.title: 5. The schedule
docs.text:
The schedule is one Dart file. Each task is a plain function, or a job.

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:team/app/jobs/send_daily_summary.job.dart';
import 'package:team/app/models/task/task.model.dart';
import 'package:team/app/services/user.service.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  /// every morning, put one summary job per user on the queue
  s.call('daily-summary', queueSummaries).weekdays().dailyAt('08:00');

  /// at night, delete tasks that were done more than 90 days ago
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00').withoutOverlapping();

  /// remove failed jobs older than 2 days
  s.command('queue:prune-failed', args: <String>['--hours=48']).daily();
}

Future<void> queueSummaries() async {
  List<int> ids = await Dox().ioc.get<UserService>().idsWithOpenTasks();
  for (int id in ids) {
    await SendDailySummary(userId: id).dispatch();
  }
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  DateTime before = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 90));
  await Task().where('done_at', '<', before).delete();
}
  • The scheduler does the timing. The queue does the work. The summary task only puts jobs on the queue, so 1,000 users do not block the scheduler.
  • timezone reads 08:00 in your zone, not in UTC.
  • withoutOverlapping() skips a run while the last one still runs.
  • Each task runs once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule. With many servers, use a Redis cache store for the locks.

See the next run of each task:

dox schedule:list

Run one task now, to try it:

dox schedule:test cleanup

docs.title: 6. Run the worker and the scheduler
docs.text:
In dev, run three processes:

dox s
dox queue:work --queue=emails,default
dox schedule:work

--queue=emails,default works both queues. The first one goes first.

In production, dox build makes binaries for all three in build/bundle/bin. Run them next to each other. For example with Docker Compose:

services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4
  scheduler:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/schedule work
  • --concurrency=4 runs four jobs at once. It helps for jobs that wait, like email and HTTP calls.
  • On docker stop, the worker takes no new job and waits for the running ones.
  • The worker keeps your code in memory. Restart it on each deploy.

For a small app, you can skip the extra processes. QueueConfig(inProcess: true) runs jobs inside the web server, and ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true) runs the schedule there too. Use separate processes when the jobs get heavy, so they do not slow down your API.

docs.title: 7. Failed jobs
docs.text:
When handle() throws, the worker waits the backoff time and tries again. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and failed() runs.

dox queue:failed          # list them
dox queue:retry <id>      # put one back on its queue
dox queue:retry all       # put all back

Dart can not stop a running Future. After a timeout, the try counts as failed, but the code can keep running. So write jobs that are safe to run twice.

docs.title: 8. Test it
docs.text:
Queue.fake() records each dispatch, and runs nothing. Mail.fake() does the same for email. A queued email goes to mail.queued, not to the job queue:

late QueueFake queue;
late ArrayTransport mail;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
  mail = Mail.fake();
});

tearDown(() {
  Queue.restore();
  Mail.restore();
});

test('sign up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await userService.signUp(const SignUp(name: 'Ann', email: 'ann@example.com'));
  mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome to the team');
  mail.assertNothingSent();
});

test('the morning task queues one summary per user', () async {
  await queueSummaries();
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendDailySummary>(2);
});

To test the job itself, call handle():

await SendDailySummary(userId: 1).handle();

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Requests answer at once. Slow work runs in a worker.
  • Retries, delays and failed jobs with no extra code.
  • The schedule in Dart, in one file, with time zones.
  • Each scheduled task runs once, on one server or many.
  • Fakes for the queue and mail, so tests need no Redis and no SMTP.

docs.title: Build a Dart API with Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to go from an empty folder to a tested API with a database, validation and a native binary, in a few short steps.

Each step has a small code block and a link to its docs page. The code comes from the tutorial, which builds a small blog API.

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI and make a project
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer.

dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get

dox create downloads the starter project and makes a .env file with a new random APP_KEY. The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

Docs: Installation

docs.title: 2. Start the server
docs.text:
dox s

dox s is short for dox serve. It runs the code generator and the server. It restarts the server when you save a .dart file.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/ping

pong

Docs: Step 1: Create the project

docs.title: 3. Make a model and a migration
docs.text:
Stop dox s first with Ctrl+C. dox s restarts the server when a new file appears, and the server runs new migrations at start. So it would run the new migration before you add the columns.

One command makes the model and the migration:

dox make:model Post -m

Add the columns to the migration:

db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart
await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body');
  table.timestamps();
});

Add the same fields to the model:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}

Then run the migration:

dox migration:run

Then start dox s again. The server also runs new migrations each time it starts. For relations and more queries, read Dart ORM with migrations in Dox.

Docs: Step 2: Model and migration, Model

docs.title: 4. Add a controller and routes
docs.text:
dox make:controller Post -r

A controller method can return a model or a list of models. Dox sends it as JSON.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

One line adds the routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.resource('posts', PostController);

Route.resource makes a route for each method the controller has. Here that is GET /api/posts and GET /api/posts/{id}. Dox makes the controller for you, because it has @Inject().

Docs: Step 3: Routes and controller, Routing

docs.title: 5. Check the input with a DTO
docs.text:
dox make:dto SavePost

A DTO is a class with rules on its fields:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

Ask for it as a parameter in the controller:

Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
  Post post = Post()
    ..title = body.title
    ..body = body.body;
  await post.save();
  return response(post).statusCode(201);
}

Dox checks the body before the method runs. Your code gets a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 answer with one message for each field:

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}

Add two lines to lib/config/app.dart, so the app knows the DTOs:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ... the rest stays the same
);

Docs: Step 4: Validation, Validation

docs.title: 6. Write a test
docs.text:
DoxTestClient starts the app inside the test, on a free port.

test/http_test.dart
void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/posts gives a list', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/posts');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectJson(isA<List<dynamic>>());
  });
}

dart test

The full test in the tutorial also runs the migrations first, so it works on an empty database.

Docs: Step 6: Test, Testing

docs.title: 7. Build one binary
docs.text:
dox build

dox build runs the code generator, then compiles the app. The result is in build/bundle. bin/server is one native binary. It does not need the Dart SDK.

cd build/bundle
cp ../../.env .env
./bin/server

The project also has a Dockerfile that builds the same bundle into a small image.

Docs: Step 7: Build and deploy, Docker

docs.title: What you have now
docs.text:
• A server that restarts when you save a file.
  • A database table, a model and a migration.
  • Routes and a controller that return JSON.
  • Input checks with a typed DTO and a 422 answer for bad input.
  • A test that runs the real app.
  • One binary for production.

The tutorial does all of this in full, and adds login with dox_auth in step 5.

docs.title: Dart backend frameworks: how to choose
docs.text:
This post compares five Dart backend options, Serverpod, Dart Frog, Shelf, Vania and Dox, by what each one includes, so you can pick the one that fits your app.

You know Dart, maybe from Flutter, and now you need a server. The articles we found compare only three options, and they rarely check what a real backend needs: a database, migrations, background jobs and mail. This post does.

We build Dox, so we are not neutral. That is why every fact about another project links to its own docs, GitHub or pub.dev page.

In brief

Pick by what your app needs.

  • You want a typed client made for your Flutter app: Serverpod.
  • You want a small API with few parts: Dart Frog or Shelf.
  • You want routes, an ORM, migrations, queues, mail and auth in one framework: Dox or Vania.

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
• Serverpod: pick it if your client is a Flutter app and you want the client code made for you. It also has a hosted service, Serverpod Cloud.
  • Dart Frog: pick it if you want a small, simple framework with routes from files.
  • Shelf: pick it if you want to build your own stack from small parts.
  • Vania: pick it if you want a full framework and you use MongoDB or MySQL.
  • Dox: pick it if you want a full framework with typed input, queues, mail and a scheduler, on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite.

docs.title: Four kinds of Dart backend
docs.text:
The options are not all the same kind of thing. You can put them on one line, from "you pick every part" to "most parts come with it":

  1. LibraryShelf, Relic
  2. Small frameworkDart Frog
  3. Full-stack with a clientServerpod
  4. Full backend frameworkDox, Vania
  1. A library is the base layer. It gives you the request, the response and middleware. You add the router, the database and the rest.
  2. A small framework is a library plus routing, a CLI and a dev server. You still add the database and other parts.
  3. A full-stack framework with a client is built for one kind of client. It makes the server and the client code from one place.
  4. A full backend framework is the largest kind. It includes the database layer, migrations, auth, mail and more. It does not care which client calls it.

None of these is better in general. A library is the right choice when you want control. However, a full framework saves time when you do not want to pick and connect many packages, such as a driver, a migration tool, a queue and a mailer.

docs.title: Serverpod
docs.text:
Serverpod is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server. Serverpod then generates a typed Dart client, and your Flutter app calls the server like a local function.

What it is good at:

  • The generated client. You do not write HTTP calls or JSON parsing by hand for your endpoints.
  • Many years of use. It has been on pub.dev since 2021.
  • A hosted service. Serverpod Cloud deploys your server and its database for you.
  • A lot built in: an ORM with migrations, many login providers, caching, file uploads and future calls for work that runs later.

When it may not fit:

  • Your database is MySQL or MongoDB. Serverpod uses Postgres and SQLite. In contrast, Dox and Vania support MySQL, and Vania supports MongoDB.
  • Many of your clients are not Flutter apps. The generated client is Dart.
  • The license matters to you. The main serverpod package uses the SSPL. Most other packages use BSD-3.

docs.title: Dart Frog
docs.text:
Dart Frog is a small backend framework built on Shelf. Each file in the routes/ folder is a route. The dart_frog CLI makes a project, runs a dev server with hot reload, and makes a production build.

What it is good at:

  • It is simple. There are few concepts to learn.
  • File-based routes. The folder tree shows your whole API.
  • Small add-on packages for auth and WebSocket.

Things to know:

  • There is no database layer. For example, you pick your own Postgres driver and write your own migrations.
  • The project moved to the dart-frog-dev group in 2025. See the post by Very Good Ventures.
  • The last dart_frog release on pub.dev is 1.2.6, from November 2025.

docs.title: Shelf (and Relic)
docs.text:
Shelf is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework. You add shelf_router for routes, and then you pick every other part yourself.

Shelf is a good choice when you want full control, or when you build a small service with one job. Dart Frog is built on it.

Relic is a newer web server from the Serverpod team. Its README says it is "inspired by Shelf", with typed headers, its own router and WebSocket support. Serverpod's own web server is built on it. Like Shelf, it is not a full framework.

docs.title: Vania
docs.text:
Vania is a full backend framework. Its README calls it "a batteries-included backend framework for Dart".

What is in the core package: routing, middleware, validation, an ORM with relations, migrations, seeders, sessions, a cache, mail, file storage and an IoC container. Auth, OpenAPI, Redis and WebSocket rooms come as add-on packages.

What it is good at:

  • MongoDB. It has drivers for MySQL, MariaDB, Postgres and MongoDB, behind one database API.
  • A full CLI. vania create, vania serve with hot reload, make:* commands, migrations and vania build.
  • Recent releases. Version 2.1.0 came out in October 2026.

Things to know:

  • A queue and a scheduler are not in their docs.
  • Validation rules are written as strings or fluent rules, not as typed fields on a class. See their validation page.
  • There is no SQLite driver package in their docs.

docs.title: Dox
docs.text:
Dox is a full backend framework, and the one we build. dox create makes a project with routes, the ORM, migrations, a queue, a scheduler, a cache and file storage. dox add adds more packages, like mail, auth and Socket.IO.

The part we like most is typed input. You write a @Dto class, and your controller gets a checked, typed object:

lib/app/dtos/save_task/save_task.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'save_task.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class SaveTask {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  final int projectId;

  const SaveTask({required this.title, required this.projectId});

  static const DtoSchema<SaveTask> schema = $SaveTaskDto;
}
lib/app/http/controllers/task.controller.dart
@Inject()
class TaskController {
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SaveTask body) async {
    Task task = Task()
      ..title = body.title
      ..projectId = body.projectId;
    await task.save();
    return response(task).statusCode(201);
  }
}
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/tasks', (TaskController c) => c.store);

When title is too short or project_id is missing, the client gets a 422 with the errors, and store does not run. Task is a model, made with dox make:model Task -m. The same DTO also feeds the OpenAPI docs, and you can share it with a Flutter app.

What it is good at:

  • Many parts in one place: ORM, migrations, auth, queue, mail, scheduler, cache and storage.
  • Four SQL databases: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. A new project uses SQLite, so you install nothing to start.
  • Any client. It is a plain HTTP API with OpenAPI docs, so web, mobile and other servers can call it.
  • One binary. dox build makes a native binary for your server.

docs.title: When not to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want a long track record. Dox has been on pub.dev since 2023, but version 3 came out in October 2026. Serverpod, Dart Frog and Shelf have more years of real use.
  • You want the Dart client made for you. Dox does not generate a Dart client. It makes an OpenAPI document, and you can share DTO classes with Flutter.
  • You want a hosted service. Dox has none. You deploy it yourself, with a binary or Docker.
  • You use MongoDB. Dox supports SQL databases only.
  • You want very few parts. Dart Frog or Shelf are smaller.

More gaps are listed on What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: How to choose: five questions
docs.text:
1. Do you want a client made for your Flutter app? Yes: start with Serverpod.
  2. Do you need a database with migrations? Yes: look at Dox, Serverpod or Vania. Dart Frog and Shelf need a separate package.
  3. Do you need background jobs, mail or scheduled tasks? Dox has all three. Serverpod has future calls for jobs and schedules. Vania has mail.
  4. Which database do you use? Postgres: Dox, Serverpod or Vania. SQLite: Dox or Serverpod. MySQL or MariaDB: Dox or Vania. MongoDB: Vania.
  5. Do you want a long track record, or are you fine with a newer project? Long track record: Shelf, Serverpod or Dart Frog. Newer is fine: Dox and Vania are options too.

docs.title: Is Dart good for backend development?
docs.text: Yes, for a team that already knows Dart. You use one language on the server and in the Flutter app, and you can share code between them. The server ecosystem is smaller than the one for Node.js or Go, so some packages you may want do not exist yet.

docs.title: Can I share models between Flutter and the server?
docs.text: Yes, with all five. You put the classes in a plain Dart package that both apps use. Serverpod generates this package for you. In Dox, you put @Dto classes in a shared package, so the app and the server check input with the same rules. See Share code with Flutter.

docs.title: Does Dox replace Serverpod?
docs.text: No. They have different goals. Serverpod is built around a Flutter client. Dox is a general backend for any client. If the generated client is what you want most, Serverpod is the better fit.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Pick a library (Shelf) or a small framework (Dart Frog) when you want control and few parts.
  • Pick Serverpod when your client is Flutter and you want the client made for you.
  • Pick a full backend framework (Dox or Vania) when you want the database, jobs, mail and auth in one place.

Want to try Dox? The tutorial builds a small API with a database, validation, login and tests. For a shorter path, read Build a Dart API with Dox or A tour of Dox features.

docs.title: Dart ORM with migrations: models, relations and queries
docs.text:
This post shows how to use the Dart ORM in Dox: make two tables with migrations, write the models, connect them with relations, and read and save rows with typed queries.

A backend needs more than a database driver. It needs a way to change the tables with time, a class for each table, and a safe way to load related rows. In Dox, these parts come in two packages, dox_orm and dox_migration, and a new project has both from the start.

The example is a team app with projects and tasks. A project has many tasks, and a task belongs to one project. All code in this post was tested with dox_orm 3.2.4 and dox_migration 3.2.4 on SQLite.

Key takeaways

  • One command makes the model and the migration. dox make:model Task -m writes both files.
  • Migrations are Dart code. Each one has an up and a down, and dox migrate runs the new ones.
  • Relations are fields. @HasMany(Task) on a list field connects the two models.
  • No N+1 queries. preload('tasks') loads the tasks of all projects with one more query.
  • Four databases. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Dart 3.13 or newer.
  • The dox CLI and a Dox app:
dart pub global activate dox
dox create team_app
cd team_app
dart pub get

A new app uses SQLite, so you do not install a database. If you are new to Dox, read Build a Dart API with Dox first.

docs.title: 1. Make the models and the migrations
docs.text:
Make a model for each table. The -m option also makes the migration:

dox make:model Project -m
dox make:model Task -m

Each command makes two files:

File What it is lib/app/models/task/task.model.dart the model db/migration/<date>_create_tasks_table.dart the migration

The date in the file name keeps the migrations in the right order.

docs.title: 2. Write the migrations
docs.text:
A migration is a small class that changes the database. up makes the change, and down undoes it. Open the new file of the projects table and add a name column:

db/migration/2026_11_27_145046_create_projects_table.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateProjectsTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('projects', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('projects');
  }
}

Then open the file of the tasks table. It has a foreign key to the projects table:

db/migration/2026_11_27_145047_create_tasks_table.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateTasksTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('tasks', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.foreignId('project_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
      table.string('title');
      table.boolean('done').defaultTo(false);
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('tasks');
  }
}

Three lines do most of the work:

  • table.id() makes an auto increment primary key.
  • table.timestamps() makes the created_at and updated_at columns, and the model fills them.
  • foreignId('project_id').constrained() makes the column and the foreign key. The table name comes from the column name: project_id gives projects.

With cascadeOnDelete(), the database deletes the tasks of a project when you delete the project. See Schema for all column types.

docs.title: 3. Write the models
docs.text:
A model is a Dart class for one table. Each @Column() field is one column, and each object is one row:

lib/app/models/project/project.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../task/task.model.dart';

part 'project.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'projects')
class Project extends ProjectGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Task)
  List<Task> tasks = <Task>[];
}
lib/app/models/task/task.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../project/project.model.dart';

part 'task.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'tasks')
class Task extends TaskGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['title', 'done'];

  @Column()
  int? projectId;

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  bool? done;

  @BelongsTo(Project)
  Project? project;
}

Some things to know:

  • The column name is the field name in snake_case, so projectId is the column project_id.
  • Each column field is nullable, because a new Task() has no values.
  • The id and the timestamps come from the generated class, TaskGenerator.
  • @HasMany(Task) and @BelongsTo(Project) are the two sides of one relation. Both use the column project_id by default.

docs.title: What fillable is for
docs.text: fillable lists the keys that a model takes from a map. A map often comes from the client, and a client can send keys that you do not expect. So a model takes no key from a map until you list it. Fields that you set in code are always saved.

docs.title: 4. Run the migrations
docs.text:
Run the new migrations, then the code generator:

dox migrate
dart run build_runner build

Migrating: 2026_11_27_145046_create_projects_table
Migrated: 2026_11_27_145046_create_projects_table
Migrating: 2026_11_27_145047_create_tasks_table
Migrated: 2026_11_27_145047_create_tasks_table

dox migrate runs only the migrations that did not run yet. The server of a new Dox app also runs them at the start. With many machines, run them in one place only. See Deploy a Dart server to production with Dox.

docs.title: 5. Save rows
docs.text:
Make a model, set its fields and call save():

Project project = Project()..name = 'Website';
await project.save();
print(project.id); // 1

createRelated() saves a task of this project and sets the foreign key for you:

Task task = await project.createRelated<Task>('tasks',
    <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Write the home page'});
print(task.projectId); // 1

'tasks' is the name of the relation field in Project.

To change a row, set a field and save again. Dox sends only the fields that changed:

task.done = true;
await task.save();

UPDATE "tasks" SET "done" = TRUE,"updated_at" = '...' WHERE "id" = 1;

docs.title: 6. Read rows
docs.text:
A model has all the query builder methods. The result is a typed object or a typed list, not a map:

Project? found = await Project().find(1);

List<Task> open = await Task()
    .where('project_id', 1)
    .where('done', false)
    .orderBy('id', 'desc')
    .get();

Values go to the database as parameters of the query, so user input in a where is safe.

For a long list, paginate returns one page and the page info:

Pagination<Task> page =
    await Task().paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 10);
print(page.total); // the number of rows that match

A controller can return a model, a list of models or a page, and Dox sends it as JSON. See Query builder for joins, groups, raw SQL and more.

docs.title: 7. Load relations with no N+1 queries
docs.text:
A relation is not loaded by default. preload() loads it for all rows of the query:

List<Project> projects = await Project().preload('tasks').get();
print(projects.first.tasks.length);

Dox runs two queries, for any number of projects:

SELECT * FROM "projects";
SELECT *,"project_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "tasks"
  WHERE "project_id" IN (1);

The loaded tasks are also in the JSON of the project, with the key tasks.

The other side works the same way:

List<Task> tasks = await Task().preload('project').get();
print(tasks.first.project?.name); // Website

docs.title: Count the related rows
docs.text:
withCount() adds the number of tasks to each project and does not load the tasks:

List<Project> projects = await Project().withCount('tasks').get();
print(projects.first.countOf('tasks')); // 2

In JSON, the key is tasks_count.

docs.title: Filter by the related rows
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps only the projects that have a task that matches:

List<Project> busy = await Project().whereHas('tasks',
    (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('done', false);
}).get();

Dox also has one-to-one, many-to-many, through and polymorphic relations. See HasMany and the other relation pages.

docs.title: 8. Keep related writes together
docs.text:
A transaction runs many queries as one unit. If the function throws, the database saves none of them:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Project project = Project()..name = 'Mobile app';
  await project.save();
  await project.createRelated<Task>('tasks',
      <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Set up the project'});
});

All models and queries inside the function use the transaction. See Transactions.

docs.title: 9. Change a table later
docs.text:
Do not edit a migration that already ran on a server. Make a new one. The name tells Dox which table it changes:

dox make:migration add_due_date_to_tasks_table
db/migration/2026_11_27_145102_add_due_date_to_tasks_table.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class AddDueDateToTasksTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('tasks', (Table table) {
      table.date('due_date').nullable();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('tasks', (Table table) {
      table.dropColumn('due_date');
    });
  }
}

Add the field to the Task model:

lib/app/models/task/task.model.dart
@Column()
DateTime? dueDate;

Then run dox migrate and the generator again.

To see which migrations ran, and to undo the last one:

dox migration:status
dox migration:rollback --step=1

See Migration for SQL migrations and the other commands.

docs.title: Which databases work
docs.text:
The code in this post ran on SQLite, the default of a new app. The same models, queries and migrations run on four databases:

Database Good for SQLite development, tests and small apps. No install Postgres production MySQL 8+ and MariaDB production

To change the database, set DB_CONNECTION and the other DB_* keys in .env. A new app skips the Postgres and MySQL drivers, so also remove the skip lines of your driver in pubspec.yaml. See Skip unused drivers.

On MySQL and MariaDB, a failed migration can not undo a CREATE, ALTER or DROP. So make one table change in each migration. Dox does not support MongoDB or other databases that are not SQL. See Database.

docs.title: Is there an ORM for Dart?
docs.text: Yes. Dox has one with models, relations, migrations, soft deletes and transactions, and a new Dox project includes it. Some other Dart backends have an ORM too. Dart backend frameworks: how to choose lists them.

docs.title: Do I write SQL for a migration?
docs.text: No, a migration is Dart code with a schema builder. You can also write a migration as a plain .sql file if your team prefers SQL.

docs.title: How do I stop N+1 queries?
docs.text: Use preload(). It loads a relation for all rows of a query with one more query. Use withCount() when you need only the number of related rows.

docs.title: Can I use the ORM in tests?
docs.text: Yes. A new app has a database test that runs the migrations on SQLite and then saves and reads a model.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• dox make:model Task -m makes a model and its migration.
  • A migration changes the tables. dox migrate runs the new ones, and the server runs them at the start.
  • @HasMany and @BelongsTo connect two models, and preload() loads the related rows with one more query.

Next, put these models behind an API. Build a Dart API with Dox adds routes, a controller and typed validation. For every model method, read Model in the docs.

docs.title: Deploy a Dart server to production with Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to deploy a Dart server to production with Dox: a native binary, a small Docker image, config from the env, HTTPS, a health check and a clean shutdown.

Your team has a Dart API that works on a laptop. Before you put it in front of users, you want to know how it is built, how it runs, how it starts again after a crash and how it stops. This post answers those questions in the order of a real deploy, and each step links to the full docs page. If you did not pick a framework yet, read Dart backend frameworks: how to choose first.

Key takeaways

  • One native binary. dox build compiles the app ahead of time. The server needs no Dart SDK.
  • A small image. The final Docker image is FROM scratch: the Dart runtime and your app, with no shell.
  • Config from the env. No secret is in the image or in git. dox env:check stops a deploy with a missing key.
  • HTTPS in two ways. Put Caddy or nginx in front, or let Dox serve HTTPS with a certificate file.
  • A clean stop. On SIGTERM, Dox lets open requests finish before the process exits.

docs.title: What a production setup looks like
docs.text:
A Dox app in production is one process that uses every CPU core. A proxy in front of it does the TLS work, and a supervisor starts the process again if it stops:

  1. Client
  2. Caddy or nginxTLS and gzip
  3. Doxa private port
  4. Database

You do not need a process manager that runs one worker for each core. Dox starts one isolate for each core that the machine or the container gives it.

By default, the Dart VM runs only 8 isolates at the same time. On a server with more than 8 cores, turn on isolateGroups. See Give each isolate its own memory.

docs.title: 1. Build a native binary
docs.text:
Dart has two ways to run code. dart run uses the JIT compiler, which is for development. For production, compile the app ahead of time (AOT) into a native binary:

dox build

The result is in build/bundle/:

File What it is bin/server the native binary. It needs no Dart SDK bin/queue the queue worker, when the app has one bin/schedule the scheduler, when the app has one lib/ the native libraries, like the database drivers db/ your migrations

Start it from the bundle folder:

cd build/bundle
./bin/server

The start log must end with (native):

[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

Never run production with dart run

The JIT compiler uses much more memory at the start and starts slower. Always build with dox build. Do not use dart compile exe, because it does not include the native libraries.

dox build makes a binary for the system it runs on. So build on Linux, in CI or in Docker, when the server is Linux.

docs.title: 2. Put it in a Docker image
docs.text:
A new Dox app has this Dockerfile. The first stage builds the bundle with the Dart SDK. The final stage holds only the Dart runtime and the bundle:

Dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then builds bin/server.dart,
# bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart into build/bundle.
RUN dart pub global activate dox
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The final file tree: /app/bin, /app/lib, /app/db, /app/storage and
# a writable /tmp (uploads bigger than 1 MB go to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/

# The AOT runtime files of the dart image plus the bundle.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

FROM scratch means the image has no shell, no package manager and no source code. That keeps the image small, and there is less in it to attack or to patch. The image of the blog API in the docs is approximately 17 MB.

Build it and run it:

docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env my-app

The Docker guide adds Postgres, a volume for uploads and a health check with Docker Compose.

docs.title: 3. Keep the config in the env
docs.text:
The image has no .env file, so no secret is in the image. Give the config as environment variables, for example with --env-file, env_file: in Compose, or the secret store of your platform:

.env
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
APP_PORT=3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=postgres
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=<a real password>

Three rules protect you here:

  • APP_KEY is your most important secret. It encrypts cookies and signs tokens. Make one key for each environment with dox key:generate.
  • A bad key stops the app. In production, Dox does not start with an empty key, a key that is not 32 characters, or a public sample key.
  • Check the env before a deploy. dox env:check prints every missing or bad key and exits with code 1, so CI stops.
dox env:check

A real environment variable wins over a .env file. See Environments for dev, staging and production config.

docs.title: 4. Run the migrations
docs.text:
A new Dox app runs the migrations in bin/server.dart, before the server takes requests. So a deploy with a new migration needs no extra step.

When you run many machines, run the migrations in one place only. For example, run dox migrate one time in CI before the new version starts. Then two machines can not migrate at the same time. See Migration, or the post Dart ORM with migrations in Dox.

docs.title: 5. Turn on HTTPS
docs.text: You have two options.

docs.title: A proxy in front
docs.text:
A proxy gets and renews the certificate, does gzip and sends http:// visitors to https://. This is the best fit for most teams. With Caddy, the full config is four lines:

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
api.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}

Then tell Dox to trust the proxy, so req.ip() is the real client IP:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);

Keep the app port private. Set APP_HOST=127.0.0.1 when the proxy is on the same machine. For nginx, see Deployment: put a proxy in front.

docs.title: HTTPS in Dox
docs.text:
Dox can also serve HTTPS with no proxy. Give it a certificate file and a key file:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  serverPort: 443,
  tls: TlsOptions(
    certificatePath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem',
    keyPath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem',
  ),
  // ...
);

This fits a small server with one app. Dox does not get or renew the certificate, so use certbot or a similar tool. Read HTTPS without a proxy in Dox for the details.

docs.title: 6. Add a health check
docs.text:
A load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes must know if the app can serve requests. Add a health route with a database check:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok"}}

When the database does not answer, the answer is 503. Your platform then stops sending traffic to that machine. See Health check for a cache check and the timeout.

docs.title: 7. Keep it running, and stop it cleanly
docs.text:
A supervisor must start the process again after a crash. In Docker Compose, that is one line:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
    restart: unless-stopped

With no Docker, use Restart=always in a systemd unit. The guide Deploy to a Linux server has the full unit file.

A deploy stops the old process. On SIGTERM, Dox does these steps in every isolate:

  1. It stops taking new connections.
  2. It lets open requests finish, for 8 seconds at most by default.
  3. It runs the shutdown() of every provider, so your own connections close.
  4. It exits with code 0.

So a user with a request in progress gets an answer, not an error. Set shutdownTimeout shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

Platform Waits docker stop 10 seconds Kubernetes 30 seconds Cloud Run 10 seconds Fly.io 5 seconds systemd 90 seconds

The default of Dox is 8 seconds. That is longer than the 5 seconds of Fly.io, so set a shorter time there, or set a longer kill_timeout in fly.toml:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 4),
  // ...
);

See Graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 8. Run the queue worker and the scheduler
docs.text:
One build has three binaries. Run each one as its own process, from the same image:

Process Command web server /app/bin/server queue worker /app/bin/queue work scheduler /app/bin/schedule work

In Compose, that is one more service with command: ["/app/bin/queue", "work"]. Only the server runs the migrations, so start the server first. A small app can run the jobs and the schedule inside the web server, with no extra process. See Background jobs and scheduled tasks in Dox.

docs.title: 9. Read the logs and catch the errors
docs.text:
In production, a new Dox app writes one JSON line for each log to stdout. Docker, systemd and every log service can read that format. Set LOG_LEVEL=warn to keep only warnings and errors.

To send errors to your error tracker, extend ExceptionHandler:

lib/app/exception_handler.dart
class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    // send it to your error tracker
  }
}
lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
);

Every error that is not an HTTP exception goes to report. In production, the client sees no error details. See Error handling.

docs.title: Where to deploy
docs.text:
The same image runs on any platform that runs a container. The docs have a guide for each of these:

Target Good for Guide Your own Linux server full control, low cost Deploy to a Linux server Docker Compose the app and Postgres on one machine Docker Fly.io a managed platform with volumes Deploy to Fly.io Google Cloud Run managed HTTPS, no server to manage Deploy to Google Cloud Run

docs.title: What Dox does not do for you
docs.text:
A team that checks a framework for production must also know the limits:

  • No hosted service. You deploy the app yourself, on your server or your cloud.
  • No automatic certificates. A proxy or certbot gets the certificate.
  • No backup tool. Use pg_dump, mysqldump or the snapshots of your database service, and test a restore.
  • No deploy tool. For a deploy with no downtime, run two processes behind the proxy and restart one at a time.

More gaps are on What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: Before your first deploy
docs.text:
Go through this short list. The production checklist has the full one.

  • The app runs from dox build, and the start line says (native).
  • APP_KEY is set, secret and different in each environment.
  • dox env:check passes in CI.
  • No .env file is in the image or in git.
  • HTTPS is on, and the app port is private.
  • trustedProxies is set when a proxy is in front.
  • /health checks the database.
  • isolateGroups is on when the server has more than 8 cores.
  • A supervisor starts the process again.
  • shutdownTimeout is shorter than the kill timeout of the platform.
  • Uploads are on a volume or in S3.
  • The database has backups, and you tested a restore.

docs.title: Do I need the Dart SDK on the server?
docs.text: No. dox build makes a native binary and puts the Dart runtime next to it in the image. The SDK is only in the build stage.

docs.title: Do I need nginx in front of a Dart server?
docs.text: No, but a proxy is the best fit for most teams. Caddy or nginx gets the certificate, does gzip and sends http:// visitors to https://. Dox can serve HTTPS itself when you give it a certificate file.

docs.title: How many processes do I run?
docs.text: One for each machine. One Dox process uses every core, so you do not need one process for each core. Run more processes only for more machines, or to restart with no downtime.

docs.title: Can a Dart server run on Kubernetes?
docs.text: Yes. It is a normal container: it reads config from the env, has a health route for probes and stops cleanly on SIGTERM. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than shutdownTimeout.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Build with dox build, and run the binary in a FROM scratch image.
  • Give the config through the env, and check it with dox env:check.
  • Turn on HTTPS, add a health route and let a supervisor start the process again.

To see the full path with one app, follow Build and deploy in the tutorial. If you do not have an app yet, start with Build a Dart API with Dox. For speed and memory numbers with the method, read What makes Dox fast.

docs.title: Dox 3.1 is out
docs.text:
Dox 3.1 adds new routing tools, request helpers, new ORM features, access tokens, a new MCP package, mail and queue features, and many security and bug fixes.

This post covers 3.1.0 (November 8) and the two patch releases after it, 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 (November 9). A change that came in a patch has its version after it, like "(3.1.1)". Everything else came in 3.1.0.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Update the dox CLI:

    dox update

  2. In your pubspec.yaml, set the Dox packages to ^3.1.0 (or newer), then get them:

    dart pub upgrade

  3. Make the generated code again. Relations and DTOs get new code in 3.1.

    dox build_runner:build

  4. Read the next section. Some changes need a code change.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text: These changes can change how your app works.

docs.title: ORM
docs.text:
• Models are guarded by default. guarded is now ['*']. A model with no fillable list throws MassAssignmentException when create(), update(), insert(), upsert(), firstOrCreate() or a similar method gets a map. Before, it took every key, so User().create(req.body) could set id or is_admin. To fix it, add fillable with the columns a map may set. Or set guarded to const <String>[] to take every key, as before. save() and fields you set in code do not change. See Mass assignment.
  • A write with no key and no where() throws. Blog().delete(), Blog().update({...}), forceDelete(), increment() and decrement() on a model with no primary key value and no where() used to change every row of the table. Now they throw a StateError and run no query. To change every row on purpose, use Blog().whereRaw('1 = 1').delete() (or .update()). restore() on a query with no where() throws too.
  • findOrFail() and firstOrFail() answer 404, not 500. ModelNotFoundException is now an HTTP exception with code 404. Its constructor is no longer const.
  • A digit in a model name gets no _. Address2 now gives the table address2, the foreign key address2_id, the pivot table address2_tag and the count key address2_count. Before, it was address_2. If you use these default names, rename the table or column, or set tableName, foreignKey and the pivot names by hand.
  • New many to many methods on every model: attach, detach, sync, syncWithoutDetaching, toggle, updateExistingPivot and pivot. A @Scope() with one of these names is hidden when you call it right on a model, like Song().sync(). Rename such a scope.
  • A nullable list relation is [] after a preload with no rows, not null. For example List<Tag>? tags. Run build_runner again.
  • @Unique trusts the database. On MySQL and MariaDB, text compares without case. So TAKEN@dox.dev now fails @Unique when taken@dox.dev is in the table.
  • update() and delete() with groupBy() or having() throw an ArgumentError. The SQL was never valid.

docs.title: Routing and core
docs.text:
• RateLimit counts are shared by all isolates (without Redis). max now holds for the whole server, not for each isolate. An app with more than one isolate gets a lower real limit than before. Raise max if you need the old number.
  • Route.mount matches whole path parts. A mount at /admin gets /admin and /admin/..., but no longer /administrator. When two mount prefixes match, the longest one wins. Before, the first one added won.
  • Removed helpers: getDoxRequest and middlewareAndControllerHandler are gone from dox_core. They were not used. Use DoxRequest.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• IpRule is no longer a RegexRule, so IpRule().pattern is gone.
  • v.string().ip() now takes IPv6 too, like @Ip. Its JSON Schema is anyOf IPv4 and IPv6.
  • ip() and @Ip now say no to IPv4 addresses with leading zeros, like 01.1.1.1.
  • alphaDash() and @AlphaDash now allow digits, like post-123. The message and the JSON Schema pattern change too.
  • email() now takes + and ' before the @, like ann+tag@x.com.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
• dox exits with code 1 when there is no command, an unknown command, bad arguments, or a command that throws. Before, it exited with 0.
  • dox make:model Post now writes @DoxModel(table: 'posts'), the same plural table that -m makes. The new model has an empty fillable list.
  • migration:fresh, migration:reset, migration:refresh, migration:rollback and key:generate ask first when APP_ENV=production and you run them in a terminal. --force skips the question. Without a terminal (CI, deploy scripts), they print a warning and run as before.
  • dox make:serializer makes the file in lib/app/serializers/, not lib/app/http/serializers/ (3.1.1).

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text:
• Queue: deploy the queue worker together with the web app. An old worker does not know the new built-in mail job, so it fails queued emails. dox_queue now depends on dox_mailer.
  • Custom queue drivers: release() must now also save job.payload, so the worker can keep the exception count. The new clear() and pruneFailed() throw an UnsupportedError on a custom driver that does not override them.
  • Storage: url() on a local disk with no url option gives /storage/<path>. Before, it threw. New signed URLs include the disk name, so they do not work on 3.0.1. During a rolling deploy, they can get 403 until they expire. A signed Storage.route() on a disk that is not local still gives 403, and now also reports an UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Mail: Attachment.fromFile reads the file when the message is sent or queued, so a missing file now throws from send().
  • Views: components always get $slot and $slots.main, as empty text when there is no body. So {{ $slots.main ?? 'x' }} no longer prints x. An empty SafeString is false in @if.
  • OpenAPI: a route with an optional param, like /greet/{name?}, gives two paths: /greet/{name} and /greet. The short path gets its own summary and operation id.
  • Inertia: an empty 200 answer to an Inertia request now goes back to the page it came from.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
• Route.match(methods, path, handler) and Route.any(path, handler).
  • Route.redirect(from, to) (302) and Route.permanentRedirect(from, to) (301).
  • .where(param, regex): the route matches only when the param matches the regex. The value is checked after % decoding, and a leading ^ and trailing $ are fine.
  • Route.fallback(handler) answers a GET or HEAD that matches no route. It follows the group prefix, also one with a param like {tenant}.
  • Route.staticFiles(prefix, folder, maxAge:) serves a folder, with ETag, Last-Modified, 304 and Range support. Files in .well-known are served too. The folders reach every isolate.
  • MethodOverride middleware: a plain HTML form can reach Route.put, Route.patch and Route.delete with a _method field. MethodOverride(header: true) also reads the X-HTTP-Method-Override header.
  • Route.mount(prefix, handler, middleware: true) runs the global middleware before a raw handler.
  • Route.websocket(maxMessageSize:).
  • AppConfig.idleTimeout and AppConfig.maxConnections for the server.
  • In development, a warning when a middleware returns null.
Route.redirect('/home', '/');
Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).where('id', '[0-9]+');
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');
Route.fallback((DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Page not found'}).statusCode(404);
});

Docs: Routing, Static files, Native server

docs.title: Requests and responses
docs.text:
• req.input(key, defaultValue) with dot keys, like user.name or items.0.id.
  • filled, exists, missing, except, boolean and integer.
  • file(key) and hasFile(key) for uploads.
  • bearerToken(), path(), fullUrl(), pathIs(pattern) and routeIs(pattern). pathIs() cleans the path like the router, so /admin/ and /admin// match admin.
  • req.auth?.id() gives the id of the logged-in user.
  • SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value) loads a session with no request, for a Socket.IO login.
  • DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value) decrypts a cookie value.
  • RequestBody and BodyKind are exported, so req.requestBody.kind can tell invalid JSON from no body (3.1.1).
  • ValidationException.issues keeps every issue of a failed check, for your own 422 shape (3.1.1).
  • RequestFile.head keeps more bytes of an upload, so image size checks work.

Docs: Request, Session

docs.title: Security, encryption and cache
docs.text:
• WebSocket Origin check: Route.websocket(allowedOrigins: [...]) or AppConfig.webSocketAllowedOrigins. It is off by default. A WebSocket route with no check prints a warning at start.
  • A warning when CORS has origin * together with credentials: true.
  • Crypt.encryptString, Crypt.decryptString, Crypt.encrypt and Crypt.decrypt with the APP_KEY. A value that can not be decrypted throws DecryptException (400).
  • Hash.check, the same as Hash.verify.
  • Hash.sha256(value) to store API keys and tokens as a hash (3.1.1). Do not use it for passwords.
  • Cache().many(keys) and Cache().putMany(values).
  • Cache().flexible takes a null stale: it keeps the last good value until a refresh replaces it (3.1.1).
  • The file cache driver can delete old files by itself, with the prune_every option.

Docs: Encryption, Hashing, Cache

docs.title: Validation and DTOs
docs.text:
• New rules, each as a fluent rule and a DTO annotation: same / @Same, confirmed / @Confirmed, requiredIf / @RequiredIf, requiredWith / @RequiredWith, json / @Json, digits / @Digits, digitsBetween / @DigitsBetween, dateFormat / @DateFormatted and password / @Password.
  • between(1, 10) on v.int() and v.num().
  • exists('teams') and unique('users', column: 'email') in fluent schemas. The ORM answers them.
  • File rules: maxSize, minSize / @MinSize, mimes, mimeTypes / @MimeTypes and dimensions / @Dimensions. The MIME type is checked against the real file bytes.
  • hexColor() / @HexColor() (3.1.1).
  • @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) reads "" as null (3.1.1).
  • @OrDefault() gives a field its default for a bad value, not an error. Use it for query strings like ?page=abc (3.1.1).
  • @Describe('...') puts a description in the JSON Schema of a field and in the OpenAPI docs (3.1.2).
  • @Dto(messages:) matches the full dotted path first, like tags.*.required.
  • RuleContext.sibling('key') reads another key of the same object.
  • ImageSize.read(head), FileTypes.matchesMimeTypes and FileTypes.extensionsOf for your own file rules.
  • The build stops with a clear error when a rule names a Dart field instead of its input key.
@Dto()
class Register {
  @Describe('Shown on the profile page.')
  @Length(min: 1, max: 40)
  final String name;

  @Password(min: 8, mixedCase: true, numbers: true)
  @Confirmed()
  final String password;

  @RequiredIf('type', 'company')
  final String? vat;

  // ...
}

Docs: Validation, Validation rules

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• Many to many writes: attach(), detach(), sync(), syncWithoutDetaching(), toggle() and updateExistingPivot().
  • @ManyToMany(withPivot: [...], withTimestamps: true) reads extra pivot columns, with song.pivot['role'].
  • Polymorphic relations: @MorphMany, @MorphOne and @MorphTo, with Model.morphMap().
  • Pages: simplePaginate() (no total count) and cursorPaginate() (a page after a cursor, no OFFSET).
  • Sub queries: whereIn() with a query or any Iterable (like a Set), joinSub(), leftJoinSub() and fromSub().
  • union() and unionAll(). Read a union with get(). Methods that need one row or one part, like find() or pluck(), throw a StateError on a union.
  • Dates: whereDate(), whereTime(), whereYear(), whereMonth() and whereDay().
  • JSON: whereJsonContains() and whereJsonDoesntContain().
  • whereNot(column, value), orWhereNot(), unless() and whenValue().
  • first() and doesntExist(), the same as getFirst() and hasNoRows().
  • insertGetId(), insertMany() and insertOrIgnore().
  • onlyTrashed(), touch(), touchQuietly() and replicate().
  • withAvg(), withMin() and withExists().
  • forceCreate(), forceUpdate(), forceFill() and Model.unguarded() skip fillable and guarded. Do not pass user input to them. forceFill() throws an ArgumentError when it can not set a column.
  • toRawSql() gives the SQL with the values in it, for logs.
  • ConnectionConfig.logRedact hides values, like passwords, in the query log. Each named connection uses its own list.
  • FileQueryPrinter(buffered: true) writes the query log in the background.
  • Schema helpers: foreignIdFor(), ulid(), foreignUlid(), year(), ipAddress(), softDeletesTz(), nullableMorphs(), uuidMorphs(), dropTimestamps(), dropSoftDeletes(), dropConstrainedForeignId(), dropPrimary(), renameIndex(), fullText(), nullOnUpdate() and restrictOnUpdate().
  • Postgres with useSSL: true prints a warning that the server certificate is not checked. Set extra['sslMode'] = 'verify-full' to check it.
  • MySQL: the new sslRootCert option (URL option ssl_ca) trusts a private CA. Without TLS, it prints a warning that it is ignored.
  • MySQL: a pool that can not open now says why.
  • find(5, null) throws a clear ArgumentError: the first arg must be a column name.
  • package:dox_migration/env.dart exports loadEnv.
// many to many
PivotSyncResult result = await artist.sync('songs', <int>[1, 2, 3]);

// a page after a cursor
CursorPagination<Blog> page = await Blog()
    .orderBy('id')
    .cursorPaginate(perPage: 10, cursor: req.input('cursor'));

Docs: Query builder, Model, Many to many, Polymorphic, Schema, Pagination

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• Access tokens, opt-in. A token looks like oat_<id>.<secret>. The table keeps only a hash of the secret. Each token has a name, abilities and an expiry.
  • dox auth:tokens-table writes the migration for the access tokens table.
  • AuthMiddleware(guards: ['web', 'api']) tries several guards in order.
  • AuthMiddleware(optional: true) lets guests through too, so req.can() works on a public page.
  • GuestMiddleware lets only guests through, for login and register pages.
  • Auth().check(), Auth().id(), Auth().guest() and Auth().once(credentials).
  • Auth().userFromToken(token) and Auth().userFromSession(session) check a login with no request, like in Socket.IO.
  • Opt-in login throttle: Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle(...). Give the ip with Auth(ip: req.ip()).
  • Opt-in JWT revocation: JwtAuthDriver(revocation: true), with revokeToken, revokeAllTokens and forgetUser.
  • Opt-in small JWT: JwtAuthDriver(minimalPayload: true) puts only the user id in the token.
  • Auth.needsRehash(hash) and Auth.hashCost(hash) to raise the password hash cost.
  • JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req) reads the token. AuthDriver.reportError() reports errors.
  • New JWTs carry a jti claim. Tokens made before still work.
  • The error of logout() on a token guard now says to use revokeToken().

No auth change is breaking. Apps work the same with no code change, and no user is logged out.

AccessToken token = await Auth(guard: 'api').createAccessToken(
  user,
  name: 'cli',
  abilities: <String>['posts:read'],
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30),
);
return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value}; // shown only once

Docs: Authentication

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
dox_mcp is a new package. It turns a Dox app into an MCP server, so AI tools can call your code.

  • McpServer (Streamable HTTP), McpTool with dox_validation input schemas, McpTool.of, McpToolResult and McpContext.
  • SignedMcpSessions: session ids signed with the APP_KEY.
  • McpOAuth: the OAuth 2.1 sign-in of the MCP spec, with PKCE and dynamic client registration (3.1.1). From 3.1.2, the code_verifier, code_challenge and redirect address are checked strictly.
  • McpDtoTool<T>: a tool that takes a @Dto class as its input. handle gets the typed object. McpToolResult.invalidArguments() gives the error result for bad arguments (3.1.2).
class CreateCategory extends McpDtoTool<NewCategory> {
  @override
  String get name => 'create_category';

  @override
  String get description => 'Add a category.';

  @override
  DtoSchema<NewCategory> get dto => NewCategory.schema;

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> handle(NewCategory input, McpContext context) async {
    return McpToolResult.text('Added ${input.name}.');
  }
}

Docs: MCP

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
• Queue.fake() for tests, with assertPushed, assertPushedTimes, assertNotPushed and assertNothingPushed.
  • Job settings: retryUntil, maxExceptions and failOnTimeout.
  • dispatch(delayUntil: DateTime), dispatchIf() and dispatchUnless().
  • Worker flags: --backoff, --max-jobs, --max-time, --memory and --timeout-grace.
  • Commands: dox queue:clear, dox queue:restart, dox queue:prune-failed and dox queue:table.
  • ShouldBeEncrypted: save the job data encrypted with the APP_KEY.
  • A built-in job sends Mail.queue() and Mail.later().
  • QueueConfig.redisFromEnv() reads the Redis server from REDIS_URL, or from REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_USERNAME, REDIS_PASSWORD and REDIS_TLS.

Docs: Queue

docs.title: Mail and notifications
docs.text:
• Mailables: one class per kind of email, with send(), queue() and later().
  • Markdown mail, from a dox_view template. A text value from data stays text. Pass a SafeString to put Markdown from a value.
  • MailMessage: an email made of lines and a button, with no template.
  • Notifications: Notification, MailChannel, Notifiable and your own channels.
  • Mail.queue() and Mail.later() send the email from the job queue. With encrypt: true, a send error in the log does not show the recipient.
  • Message.toJson() and Message.fromJson(), and the MailQueue interface with Mail.useQueue().
  • Mail.raw(), and Mail.to(...).cc(...).bcc(...).send(...).
  • Mail.alwaysTo(address) sends every email to one address, for example on staging.
  • Mail.onSending() and Mail.onSent() hooks, and Mail.clearHooks().
  • Test checks on Mail.fake(): assertSent, assertSentCount, assertNotSent, assertNothingSent, assertQueued, assertNotQueued and assertNothingQueued.

Docs: Mail, Notifications

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
• ScheduleConfig(timezone: ...): the default time zone of every task.
  • environments(['production']): run a task only in these environments.
  • unlessBetween(start, end).
  • New frequencies, like everyTwoHours, twiceDailyAt, lastDayOfMonth, quarterly, yearlyOn and mondays() to sundays().
  • A warning when onOneServer() uses a lock store that is not shared between servers.
  • Scheduler.close() frees the overlap locks.
  • When a provider's setup() throws, SchedulerRunner shuts down the providers that already started.

Docs: Scheduler

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• append(), prepend(), size(), lastModified(), makeDirectory() and directoryExists().
  • temporaryUrl(), the same as signedUrl().
  • file.store(folder, disk: 's3'), file.storeAs(folder, name) and Storage().putRequestFileAs().
  • atomic_writes: a failed upload never leaves a half-written file.
  • assertExists() and assertMissing() on a fake disk, for tests.

Docs: File storage

docs.title: Socket.IO
docs.text:
• SocketAuth logs a socket in at connect time. The user is in socket.user.
  • handshake.token, handshake.cookie(name) and await handshake.session().
  • ServerOptions(allowedOrigins:) turns on an origin check.

Docs: Socket.IO

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
• New tags: @isset, @empty, @auth, @guest, @env, @production, @once, @verbatim, @class, @checked, @selected and @disabled.
  • Components get $attributes (with merge()) and $slot.
  • ViewEngine(environment:) sets the environment for @env and @production. By default it is APP_ENV.

Docs: Views

docs.title: Inertia
docs.text:
• Inertia.render(), the same as inertia(), and Inertia.lazy, the same as Inertia.optional.
  • Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value) shares a prop with every page.
  • A deferred prop can be merged: Inertia.defer(fn).merge().
  • The asset version is checked before the controller runs, so an old page gets 409 at once.
  • The root view and the Vite manifest are kept in memory.
  • A prop that can not become JSON gives an error that names the prop and its type.

Docs: Inertia

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
• paramResponses on RouteDoc: answers that only happen when the path has a param, like 404.
  • namedResponses: responses with a text key, like default or 2XX.
  • The body of a GET or DELETE route goes in the query string.

Docs: OpenAPI

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
• Package commands: a package adds its own dox commands with the dox: commands: key in its pubspec.yaml. dox help lists them. They work in a pub workspace too.
  • package:dox_core/command.dart with Command and MigrationFile, to write these commands.
  • dox migrate makes bin/migrate.dart when it is missing.
  • dox key:generate --show prints a new key and writes nothing.
  • --step given twice is an error.
  • dox serve --port=... prints a warning that says to set APP_PORT.

Docs: CLI, Package commands

docs.title: App template
docs.text:
The template that dox create uses got new files too.

  • Safer Docker Compose defaults, and a queue worker service.
  • AGENTS.md and the .agents/skills/dox skill: rules and recipes for AI coding tools. CLAUDE.md points to the same files (3.1.1).
  • Serializers live in lib/app/serializers/ (3.1.2).

docs.title: Redis client
docs.text:
• RedisOptions.fromUrl(url) reads a redis:// or rediss:// URL.
  • RedisSetOption is deprecated. It was empty and not used.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• back() only follows a Referer of the same host. Before, it was an open redirect.
  • ORM guarded could be skipped with a changed key, like ' is_admin' or 'IS_ADMIN'. Now the check trims the name and ignores case.
  • A local signed URL for one disk no longer works on the route of another disk.
  • Inertia ignores the Vite public/hot file when APP_ENV is production.
  • On MySQL, a key with a letter that is not ASCII can no longer set a guarded column.
  • Postgres: an unknown verify value now means the full certificate check.

docs.title: Routing and core
docs.text:
• A bad multipart body gets 400, not 500.
  • abort() headers are kept on routes with a next middleware.
  • A mounted handler that throws gives 500. Before, the client could hang.
  • A download name with quotes or non-ASCII letters gets a safe Content-Disposition.
  • res.withHeaders and res.header no longer drop or double headers.
  • A resumed download with If-Range no longer mixes two versions of a file. If-Range is used only when it matches the file's Last-Modified date or its strong ETag.
  • A Range header sent on two lines no longer gives 500.
  • req.session.reflash() keeps the flash data on the first use of the session.

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• A model write with no key and no where() no longer changes every row.
  • blog.update({...}) on a loaded model changes only that row and sets updated_at.
  • save() keeps an updated_at that you set.
  • A soft delete and restore() set updated_at too.
  • restore() on a query restores the soft deleted rows of the query.
  • reload() and preload clear a relation when the related rows are gone.
  • find('email', null) finds the row where email is null.
  • limit() with a negative number is ignored.
  • having('x', '!=', null) builds x IS NOT NULL.
  • update() and delete() with join(), orderBy() or limit() work on Postgres and SQLite.
  • foreignId('x').unique().constrained() compiles.
  • A failed nested transaction releases its savepoint.
  • @Unique and @Exists on Postgres with a value that does not fit the column no longer give 500.
  • @name inside a quoted string or a comment is no longer read as a param on MySQL and SQLite.
  • The query log lists the values in the right order.
  • Logger.warn prints yellow.
  • Rollback goes on when the file of a migration that already ran is gone.
  • MySQL 8.4 and Postgres: a text param is no longer stored with the wrong type after a table change.
  • MySQL 8.4: the same SQL with a number param first and a text param later no longer gives wrong rows.
  • Postgres: a broken server message gives an error, not a crash of the process.
  • Postgres: a query in a transaction is not sent again after a "cached plan" error.
  • MySQL: a slow DNS lookup when a pool opens no longer stops the other isolates.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• The Bearer prefix is matched in any case.
  • A JWT check no longer hides unexpected errors. They go to the exception handler.
  • A request with two Authorization headers is a normal 401.

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text:
• Cache: FileDriver.prune() no longer deletes a value written at the same time.
  • Mail: Attachment.fromFile no longer blocks the server while it reads the file. An onError of FailoverTransport that throws no longer stops the failover.
  • Scheduler: schedule work ends a few seconds after Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. dailyAt('13') means 13:00. The overlap lock stays until the work really ends.
  • Socket.IO: CORS origin matching ignores case and a trailing /.
  • Views: {{ errors.email }} works with no session. A global named errors shows. The toJson() cache lasts one render.
  • Inertia: flash messages are kept after a deploy. A function prop inside a map or a list runs too.
  • CLI: migration:rollback --step 2 (with a space) works.
  • Redis client: the client waits for AUTH and SELECT before it sends commands. A failed AUTH on reconnect no longer crashes the app. The connect has a timeout. A server that closes the connection right after connect no longer crashes the app. The handshake tries again when the server is not ready yet (LOADING, BUSY, MASTERDOWN, TRYAGAIN). The wait between tries grows, and a long run of tries no longer ends in a stack overflow. disconnect() stops a try that is waiting.

docs.title: Full list
docs.text:
Every change is in the changelogs:

  • The Changelog page of the docs (dox_core, dox_builder, dox_annotation, dox_cache).
  • GitHub releases: dox, dox-orm, dox-auth, dox-validation, dox-mcp, dox-cli, dox-queue, dox-mailer, dox-scheduler, dox-storage, dox-socketio, dox-view, dox-inertia and dox-openapi.

docs.title: Dox 3.2 patches: faster, less memory, fewer leaks
docs.text:
This release is patch versions only. It makes Dox faster, uses less memory, and fixes memory leaks in long-running apps. There are no API changes. A few defaults changed, so read Read before you update.

Key takeaways

  • Faster ORM. A list of 100 rows as JSON is 47% faster on Postgres and 66% faster on MySQL. The query builder is 12–15% faster.
  • Faster queue. A Postgres worker runs 61% more jobs per second, and about 9 times more right after a burst of jobs.
  • Less memory. On Postgres, the ORM app uses half the peak memory (253 MB to 117 MB). A plain Dox server uses about a third less.
  • Leaks fixed. The idle queue worker, connections of clients that left, and several Socket.IO and Postgres cases no longer grow memory over time.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only, no API changes. Run dart pub upgrade and dox build_runner:build, then check Read before you update.

docs.title: Why this release
docs.text:
Some Dox apps used a bit more memory every day in production. We looked at every package for leaks and slow paths. This release fixes what we found:

  • An idle queue worker used about 8 MB more memory per day for each loop. This is fixed.
  • A request whose client went away could keep its connection open forever. This is fixed.
  • Rows from the ORM carried all the query builder state. They are much smaller now.
  • The hot path of every request does less work.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Every package with a change gets a new patch version. Packages with no change keep their version.

Package New version dox_core, dox_builder 3.2.2 dox_cache 3.2.1 dox_orm, dox_migration, dox_cache_database 3.2.2 dox_queue, dox_queue_database 3.2.2 dox_scheduler, dox_storage, dox_inertia 3.2.2 dox_socketio, dox_auth, dox_mailer 3.2.1 dox_http_native, dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native 3.2.1 ioredis 3.2.1

No change: dox_annotation, dox_validation, dox_openapi, dox_view, dox_mcp and the dox CLI.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions:

    dart pub upgrade

    Upgrade dox_core and dox_http_native together. The new dox_core uses NativeResponse.end() and headSent from the new dox_http_native.

  2. Make the generated code again. The new dox_builder writes faster model code:

    dox build_runner:build

  3. Read Read before you update. Most apps need nothing more.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
We ran the same apps on the released 3.2 packages and on this release. Same machine, same rig, one server at a time, old and new taking turns, 2 or 3 runs each. The numbers are the average of the runs.

ORM: 47% more requests, half the memory

GET /orm-list: 100 rows with a model query, as JSON. Postgres, 256 connections.

req/s p99 RAM Doxthis release 31,18347% faster 15.0 ms 117 MB Doxreleased 3.2 21,274before 27.8 ms 253 MB

Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk

Query builder: one row

GET /qb: table('world').where('id', id).first(). Postgres, 256 connections.

req/s p99 RAM Doxthis release 249,86215% faster 3.0 ms 117 MB Doxreleased 3.2 217,259before 3.3 ms 253 MB

Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk

HTTP: a bit faster, a third less memory

GET / on a full Dox app, 512 connections.

req/s p99 RAM Doxthis release 649,9905% faster 1.8 ms 21 MB Doxreleased 3.2 617,618before 1.9 ms 31 MB

Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 512 connections · wrk

RAM is the peak memory of the whole server, the median of the runs. For the database cards it is the peak over all routes of that app.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
A full Dox app with three routes, the rules of the-benchmarker. Requests per second, the average of 3 runs.
