Route Connections 3.2 This release Change GET / 64 495,089 521,583 +5% GET / 256 617,487 626,655 +1% GET / 512 617,618 649,990 +5% GET /user/:id 64 456,879 482,241 +6% GET /user/:id 256 560,239 552,170 about the same GET /user/:id 512 550,589 557,409 +1% POST /user 64 435,214 461,935 +6% POST /user 256 530,144 555,397 +5% POST /user 512 517,625 564,322 +9% Peak memory (median) 31 MB 21 MB −32%

The native server alone, with no framework (dox_http_native, average of 2 runs), has the same speed as before. It serves about 690,000 requests per second at 512 connections. That is close to the most wrk can send, so wrk is the limit here. Its peak memory went from about 30 MB to 19 MB, because connections now share one read buffer per core. See Native server.

docs.title: Database, query builder and ORM
docs.text: A small app with one table of 10,000 rows. 256 connections, requests per second, higher is better.

docs.title: Postgres 18
docs.text:
Average of 3 runs.

Test 3.2 Now Change 100 rows to JSON (ORM) 21,274 31,183 +47% Preload a relation, 20 rows 20,596 25,978 +26% 2 relations in a transaction 8,325 9,936 +19% JSON response 472,715 555,149 +17% Query builder, one row 217,259 249,862 +15% where('id', id).first() 207,500 237,464 +14% find(), then save() 95,714 105,912 +11% One row with find(id) 224,865 243,143 +8% 20 rows, one query after another 14,700 14,722 same Peak memory (median) 253 MB 117 MB −54%

docs.title: MySQL 8.4
docs.text:
Average of 2 runs.

Test 3.2 Now Change 100 rows to JSON (ORM) 18,481 30,671 +66% JSON response 518,197 598,645 +16% Query builder, one row 214,335 240,542 +12% 2 relations in a transaction 5,573 6,235 +12% where('id', id).first() 212,650 228,801 +8% One row with find(id) 222,045 238,263 +7% find(), then save() 94,271 98,262 +4% Preload a relation, 20 rows 16,933 17,460 +3% 20 rows, one query after another 11,980 12,265 +2% Peak memory (range) 253–261 MB 125–222 MB lower

We also ran the same routes with the driver alone, with no ORM (dox_postgres_native, average of 2 runs). One row went from 266,664 to 297,000 requests per second (+11%). The JSON response went from 550,049 to 592,900 (+8%).

Why the numbers moved:

  • ORM rows no longer carry the query builder state. So a list of rows is much cheaper to make, to keep in memory and to turn into JSON.
  • In a transaction, the relations of a model now load together, not one by one.
  • "20 rows, one query after another" waits for the database 20 times in a row. The database is the limit there, so it barely moves.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
20,000 jobs that do nothing, on Postgres 18, with 4 worker loops on 2 cores. Jobs per second, the average of 3 runs.

Test 3.2 Now Change Run the jobs 6,800 10,924 +61% Run the jobs right after a burst 816 7,452 about 9× Push 20,000 jobs with Queue.batch() 2.0 s 0.33 s 6× faster
  • A worker now takes a job with one statement, not a transaction of 4 round trips.
  • Queue.batch() inserts the jobs with multi-row inserts, not one insert per job.
  • "Right after a burst" is a table that was nearly empty and just got many jobs. Postgres still thinks the table is small for up to about a minute. Before, each pop then sorted every waiting job, so the worker was 10 times slower until Postgres updated its statistics. A new index fixes this. See Read before you update to add it to an old table.

How it was run: Docker on an Apple M2, linux/arm64. The server gets 2 CPUs, wrk gets the others. For the database routes, the database gets 2 CPUs of its own. wrk with keep-alive, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds per route. AOT build (dart build cli). See Performance for the full rig.

docs.title: Run heavy work off the server isolate
docs.text:
Dox().compute(task) runs heavy CPU work, like a PDF, an image or a big JSON file, on a worker isolate. The server answers other requests in the meantime. One small pool of workers is shared by every server isolate. AppConfig.computeWorkers sets its size (default 4).

Hash.makeAsync and Hash.verifyAsync now run on this pool. Before, each call started a new isolate, so 500 logins at once started 500 isolates.

Docs: Performance mistakes

docs.title: Strict mode for development
docs.text:
Strict mode warns about code that makes an app slow. It is off by default.

  • AppConfig(strict: StrictConfig(enabled: true)) warns when a route blocks the isolate longer than 50 ms, and when Hash.make or Hash.verify runs in the web server.
  • DatabaseConfig(strict: OrmStrict(enabled: true)) warns about N+1 queries (the same relation loaded row by row) and about a get() with no limit() that reads more than 1,000 rows.

Each warning says what to use instead. Turn both on in development with appConfig.isDevelopment.

Docs: Performance mistakes, App config

docs.title: Log tags
docs.text:
Every pretty log line now starts with a dim tag that says where it comes from: [request], [server], [error], [app], [db:main], [queue], [socketio], [auth], [mail] and more. The scheduler uses [scheduler] when SchedulerFlags.loggerLines is on. Pass your own tag as the third argument:

Logger.info('invoice sent', {'id': 42}, 'billing');

In JSON logs, the tag is the source field.

docs.title: Other new options
docs.text:
• CoreFlags.rateLimitIpv6Prefix (opt-in): RateLimit counts an IPv6 client by its /64 prefix. See Rate limiting.
  • fsync: false on a file cache store skips the sync to disk on each write. See Cache.
  • prune_interval on a database cache store prunes expired rows now and then.
  • --max-sleep for the queue worker: an idle worker sleeps longer, up to this time. See Queue.
  • SchedulerFlags.loggerLines (opt-in): scheduler lines go through the app Logger. See Scheduler.
  • unsigned_payload: true on an S3 disk skips the body hash (HTTPS only). See File storage.
  • Socket.IO opt-in limits: maxAttachmentBytes, maxAuthSize, maxWriteBufferSize and ackTimeout. See Socket.IO.
  • ioredis: maxQueuedCommands (opt-in) caps the commands that wait for a connect.
  • A redis cache store takes 'options': RedisOptions(...), so every ioredis option works there too, like commandTimeout or onError. Sessions and rate limits on Redis use this store. See Cache.
  • The queue worker warns once when a job may run longer than retryAfter. Then a second worker could take the same job while the first one still runs it.
  • NativeWebSocket.pingInterval now works.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
• A request with no body makes no body map until you read req.body.
  • A response makes no Future, map, set or list unless you use them.
  • CORS does not read the Origin header when it has nothing to check.
  • A route with params skips its regex when the url does not start with the route's text.
  • A JSON response starts with a 1 KB buffer, not 8 KB. Small JSON bodies encode about 2 times faster.
  • An ASCII text body is written straight to bytes.
  • The cookie session driver decrypts the cookie only when you use req.session.
  • RateLimit on Redis is one round trip per request, not two or three.

docs.title: ORM
docs.text:
• Rows no longer carry the query builder state. Each row from get() uses much less memory.
  • toJson(), preload() and relation loading do less work per row.
  • A relation load reads only the key column of each row (needs dox build_runner:build).
  • where(column, value).first() reuses the SQL of find(). The query builder does less work per query too.
  • create() and save() copy less.
  • Inside a transaction, the relations of a model load together, not one by one.

docs.title: Database drivers
docs.text:
• Postgres: each isolate gets a fair share of the connection pool. Before, under load, isolates passed connections back and forth, and the slowest requests got slower.
  • The native HTTP server uses one shared read buffer per core, not 16 KB per connection.

docs.title: Queue, cache, storage and Socket.IO
docs.text:
• Postgres queue: a worker takes a job with one statement, not a transaction of 4 round trips. Several queues are polled in one statement. An idle worker makes one round trip per poll.
  • Postgres and SQLite queue: right after a burst of jobs, a pop no longer sorts every waiting job (a new index).
  • Queue.batch() inserts its jobs with multi-row inserts.
  • Database cache store: add, increment, pull, touch and locks run one statement on Postgres and SQLite.
  • Memory cache store: removing the least recently used item is O(1), not O(n).
  • S3 putStream keeps one part in memory, not two or three (about 8 MiB in place of 24 MiB per upload). stream() and download() send one GET, not a HEAD and a GET.
  • Local disk append adds to the file, without reading and writing the whole file.
  • Socket.IO: a room broadcast with except makes no copy of the room. With the Redis adapter, a server does not decode broadcasts for rooms it does not have.
  • ioredis: text like Burmese or emoji is encoded in one pass.

docs.title: Memory leaks
docs.text:
• Queue: an idle worker leaked a listener on each sleep, about 8 MB a day per loop. This also hit the in-process worker in the web server.
  • Native HTTP: sometimes a client leaves while its request still waits, and the handler never answers (for example, a database call with no timeout). The server then kept that connection forever. The same happened to a server-sent events stream that wrote nothing after the client left. Now the connection closes after AppConfig.idleTimeout.
  • Native HTTP: response.done never completed when the client left first. A handler writing events from a timer kept its timer forever.
  • Native HTTP: accepted sockets now get TCP keep-alive, so a client that vanished with no close is found in about 2 minutes.
  • Postgres: a query that failed after its Parse left a prepared statement on the server. The Postgres backend grew with each one.
  • Postgres: each cached statement kept the whole batch of its request in memory, not only its SQL. It now keeps its own copy of the SQL.
  • Postgres, MySQL and the ORM: SQL longer than 4 KB is no longer kept in the SQL caches. Big generated inserts could fill them with hundreds of MB.
  • Socket.IO: socket.join() after a disconnect kept the socket in the room forever.
  • Socket.IO: unfinished binary packets, and broadcast acks when Redis was down, stayed in memory.
  • Scheduler: a Scheduler made without out kept every log line forever. It now keeps the last 64 KB.
  • Rate limit: the counter in the main isolate had no cap on clients. It now keeps at most 100,000.
  • ioredis: while Redis was down, every command waited forever and kept its data. Commands now time out after 10 seconds.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Socket.IO: a client could send the start of a binary packet and never the rest. The parts stayed in memory, also before the client joined a namespace. Now such a client is closed.
  • Socket.IO: a 1 MB polling body made of separators was split into about 500,000 strings at once. Now packets are read one at a time.
  • Socket.IO: with maxSessions not set, every GET request makes a session that lives about 45 seconds. The server now prints a warning at start. Set maxSessions in production.

docs.title: Disk
docs.text:
• The file cache store never cleaned up by default. Now a write starts a light prune at most once an hour. Temp files left by a crash are removed too.
  • Upload temp files are deleted when the request is handled, also on an error or a raw Route.mount handler.

docs.title: Bugs
docs.text:
• Sessions with the cache driver on a memory store lived in each isolate on its own, so users were logged out at random. They now live in the main isolate.
  • Scheduler: a slow tick that ended in the next minute skipped that minute, so a dailyAt('02:00') task could miss a day.
  • Scheduler: with inProcess: true, the schedule also ran in every bin/queue.dart process.
  • Native HTTP: a streamed answer with status 1xx, 204 or 304 broke the next answer on the same keep-alive connection.
  • Native HTTP: response.flush() did nothing. It now sends the head and the bytes so far, like dart:io.
  • Core: an error after a flush (for example in server-sent events) wrote Internal Server Error into the middle of the stream. Now the response just ends.
  • Core: a multipart body with no closing boundary kept the request open forever.
  • ORM: find('meta->n', 10) on a JSON path failed the second time on Postgres and MySQL.
  • ORM: $getRelation<User>('user') with a type threw a TypeError.
  • Database cache store: an increment past the 64-bit limit wrapped to a negative number. It is now an error.
  • S3: directoryExists was false for a folder made in the S3 console, and deleteDirectory left the folder marker.
  • ioredis: a bad reply byte from the server could crash the app.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text:
These changes can be seen by an app. Most apps need nothing.

  • Log text. Pretty log lines start with a tag, and plain warnings use tags like [server], [db] and [queue] in place of dox: warning:, [dox] or Queue:. JSON lines get a source field at the end. Check tools that match on log text.
  • ioredis commands time out after 10 seconds. Blocking commands and subscribers never time out. To turn it off: RedisOptions(commandTimeout: null).

  • Half-closed clients. A client that closed only its sending side now waits at most idleTimeout (30 seconds by default) for its answer. If such clients call slow handlers, raise it in lib/config/app.dart:

    AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  idleTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 120),
);

    See App config. - A test that starts the scheduler by hand. This only matters if you use ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true), so the schedule runs inside the web server.

    The problem it fixes: bin/queue.dart also calls setup() on every provider. So the schedule ran in the web server and again in every queue worker process, and each task ran more than once.

    Now SchedulerProvider.setup() starts the schedule only in the web server. Dox().startServer() marks the web server: it sets Dox().isWebServer = true. Your app and your HTTP tests start the server. So they need no change.

    A test that calls setup() itself, with no server, now gets no schedule. Set the flag first:

    test('the schedule runs in the server', () async {
  Dox().isWebServer = true; // new: without it, setup() does nothing
  SchedulerProvider provider = SchedulerProvider(
    schedule: appSchedule,
    config: const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true),
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
  );
  await provider.setup();
  expect(provider.scheduler, isNotNull);
  await provider.shutdown();
});
    - Queue indexes. A new jobs table on Postgres or SQLite gets better indexes. They keep a worker fast when many jobs come at once, and when many jobs are delayed. For an old table, add a migration that calls QueueTables.popIndex(schema). It adds only the indexes that are missing, and it does nothing on MySQL and MariaDB. This is optional, but we recommend it for Postgres apps that push jobs in bursts. - Rate limit cap. The RateLimit counter in the main isolate (no Redis) now keeps at most 100,000 clients. When it is full, it drops expired counts first, then the oldest ones. A dropped client starts again at 0. Most apps never reach this. - File cache clean-up. The file cache store now deletes expired files by itself, at most once an hour. It only touches files the cache made. Before, expired files (like old sessions) stayed on the disk for ever. - Database cache increment. An increment past the 64-bit int limit is now an error, and the value does not change. Before, it wrapped to a negative number. - Cache index. A new cache table gets an index on expires_at. For an old table, add it with schema.table('cache', (Table t) => t.index('expires_at')). This is optional.

docs.title: Dox 3.2 is out
docs.text:
Dox 3.2 adds dox add to set up a package with one command, read replicas, streaming queries, model dirty tracking, job batches and chains, a database cache store, broadcasting for Socket.IO, sub-minute schedules, layouts in views, and many more features and fixes.

Every Dox package is released as 3.2.0. This includes dox_http_native, dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native and ioredis. Two packages are new: dox_cache_database and dox_queue_database.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Update the dox CLI:

    dox update

  2. In your pubspec.yaml, set every Dox package to ^3.2.0, then get them. Do not mix versions.

    dart pub upgrade

  3. Make the Breaking changes that apply to your app.

  4. Make the generated code again:

    dox build_runner:build

docs.title: Update with an AI agent
docs.text:
You can also let your AI coding agent do the update. Copy this prompt into it:

Update this Dox app to Dox 3.2.

1. Read the release post: https://dartondox.dev/blog/dox-3-2/
   Follow the "How to update" steps and every item in "Breaking changes"
   that applies to this app. Also check the "Rare cases" list.
2. Set every Dox package in pubspec.yaml to ^3.2.0 and run
   `dart pub upgrade`. Make the breaking changes, then run
   `dox build_runner:build`.
3. Run `dart run skills@ get --all` to get the Dox 3.2 agent skills, and use
   them for the code changes.
4. Run `dart analyze` and `dart test`. Fix every error.
5. Do not change app behaviour that is not part of the update.
   At the end, list what you changed and anything I must check by hand,
   like log dashboards that read the old JSON field names.

docs.title: Add a package with one command
docs.text:
dox add adds a Dox package and sets it up: config files, provider, bin/ file, migrations and .env keys. It never overwrites a file, so you can run it again.

dox add orm --driver=postgres
dox add queue
dox add mailer --transport=smtp

It works for orm, queue, scheduler, mailer, cache, auth, storage, socketio, view, inertia and mcp. Each package ships its own setup command, so a package you write can have one too.

Docs: Add a package

docs.title: Opt-in flags
docs.text:
Behaviors that change old results are opt-in. Each package has a flags class. Every flag is off by default, so nothing changes until you turn one on. .all() turns on all of them.

  • CoreFlags (in AppConfig(flags: ...)): envExpand, onlyPresent, cookieDefaults, hasKeyOnly, htmlStrings, replaceHeaders, decryptServerError, cacheCopies and a flag for the shape of a 422.
  • OrmFlags (in DatabaseConfig(flags: ...)): skipCleanUpdateEvents, belongsToKeyFromRelation, pluralTableNames, createWritesNull, sumReturnsZero, selectRawAdds, groupByAdds, lastPageAtLeastOne, a Postgres column type flag, toJsonLoadedRelations, preloadUnknownThrows, updateSetsUpdatedAt and incrementFiresEvents.
  • AuthFlags (in AuthConfig(flags: ...)): forbidGuest, jsonNoRedirect and endSessionsOnPasswordChange.
  • ValidationFlags (Validator.flags = ...): emptyStringsToNull, unicodeAlpha, shortInMessage, a message key flag, dtoAllErrors, dtoRejectEmptyList and dtoMaybeRejectsEmpty.
  • CacheFlags (in CacheConfig(flags: ...)): lockThrows.

Docs: Core flags, ORM flags, Validation flags, Auth flags

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• Read replicas: ConnectionConfig(read: [...], write: {...}, sticky: ...). A plain SELECT goes to a read host. Writes, locks and transactions go to the write host. query.onWriteConnection() forces the write host.
  • Streams: query.cursor() reads rows from one query as you are ready for them, so a big result does not fill the memory. query.lazy() and lazyById() read in chunks. DBDriver.stream() is the driver call under them.
  • Cancel a running query with QueryCancelToken and query.cancelWith(token) (Postgres and MySQL).
  • Pool settings in extra: requestTimeout, maxConnectionAge, idleTimeout and serverKill.
  • Relations: @HasManyThrough and @HasOneThrough. preload('posts.comments') with a dot path, and preload(name, where) with conditions. createRelated(), saveRelated() and saveManyRelated() set the foreign key for you.
  • Dirty tracking: isDirty(), isClean(), getDirty(), getOriginal(), getChanges(), wasChanged() and wasRecentlyCreated.
  • refresh() reads the row again in place. fresh() gives a new model.
  • visibleFields (the opposite of hidden), makeHidden() and makeVisible().
  • trashed() and a new trashed model event, with onTrashed() and TrashedObserver.
  • toJson() of a many to many model has a pivot key.
  • Transactions: transaction(callback, attempts: n) runs again on a deadlock. beginTransaction() gives a transaction you commit or roll back yourself. QueryBuilder.afterCommit(callback) runs work after the commit.
  • Logging: SqlQueryBuilder().listen(listener) runs after each query. slowQueryMs logs slow queries. PrettyQueryPrinter prints each query on one line, with the values in the SQL.
  • SQLite: extra: {'background': true} runs queries in a helper isolate, so one slow query does not stop the other requests.
  • Query builder: JSON paths like where('meta->lang', 'en'), join callbacks (JoinClause), crossJoin(), orderByDesc(), reorder(), skip(), forPage(), sole(), updateOrInsert(), whereAny(), whereAll() and selectRaw(sql, params).
  • Schema: .collation(), hasColumns(), hasIndex(), disableForeignKeyConstraints(), enableForeignKeyConstraints() and withoutForeignKeyConstraints().
  • Migrations: rollback --batch=3. Migrator(flags: ...). Migration queries reach the query listeners and the slow query log.
  • Postgres and MySQL native: PgCancelToken and MysqlCancelToken, stream() in chunks, and the host and port in connect errors.
// rows one by one, with a small memory use
await for (Blog blog in Blog().orderBy('id').cursor()) {
  print(blog.title);
}

// posts, and the comments of those posts
List<User> users = await User().preload('posts.comments').get();

Docs: Replicas, Transactions, Query builder, Model, Has many through, Schema, Migration

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
• New package dox_queue_database: the database driver, batches, afterCommit, QueueTables and dox queue:table. DatabaseQueueProvider sets it up for you.
  • The generated jobs.g.dart now also lists the mail jobs of dox_mailer, so a worker knows them without extra setup.
  • QueueConfig(inProcess: true) runs a worker inside the web server. It is the same name as ScheduleConfig(inProcess:). The old name workInProcess still works, but is deprecated.
  • Job batches: Queue.batch(jobs) with then, catchError, whenComplete, progress, allowFailures() and cancel(). A batch can hold chains. They need dox_queue_database.
  • Job chains: Queue.chain(jobs). The next job is pushed when the one before is done. If one fails for good, the rest is dropped and a catch job runs.
  • Job middleware: HasMiddleware, RateLimited, WithoutOverlapping and ThrottlesExceptions.
  • Unique jobs: ShouldBeUnique and ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing.
  • InteractsWithQueue: attempts(), release(), fail() and delete() inside handle().
  • Queue events: Queue.queued(), before(), after(), released(), exceptionOccurred(), failing() and the batch events.
  • dispatch(afterCommit: true) and QueueConfig(afterCommit: true). They need dox_queue_database.
  • dispatchAfterResponse() runs a job after the response is sent.
  • Named connections: QueueConfig(connections: {...}), dispatch(connection: ...) and --connection=NAME. failed_jobs gets a nullable connection column. A table without it keeps working.
  • QueueConfig(failedAtTimestamp: true), QueueConfig(serializeSync: true) and Queue.extend(name, factory).
  • Queue.fake() keeps dispatchedSync and dispatchedAfterResponse.

Docs: Queue, Background work

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
• New package dox_cache_database: a cache store on SQLite, Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB. It keeps items, locks and sessions in a table. Register it with Dox().cache.extend('database', DatabaseCacheDriverFactory(encrypter)). dox cache:table writes the migration. A write that hits a deadlock runs again after a short wait.
  • 'encrypt': true on a store encrypts its values with the APP_KEY. It works for file, redis and the database store.
  • CacheLock.throwOnTimeout and the CacheFlags.lockThrows flag: lock.block(timeout) throws LockTimeoutException.

Docs: Cache, Cache in the app

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• RateLimit(sliding: true) uses a sliding window.
  • .env files: ${OTHER} values (with CoreFlags.envExpand) and export KEY=value lines.
  • AppConfig(htmlErrors: true) sends a small HTML error page to a client that does not want JSON. AppConfig(errorPage: ...) replaces the page.
  • Route.resource(..., parameter: 'photo') names the param of one item.
  • route() and Route.url() put a param that is not in the path into the query string. absolute: true gives the full URL.
  • Dox().addGlobalMiddleware() lets a provider add global middleware.
  • Dox().loadRoutes() gives the routes with no server. RouteData.isWebSocket marks WebSocket routes.
  • res.header(k, v, replace: true), and session.regenerate(keepToken: true).
  • ServerTiming middleware, ServerTiming.add() and ServerTiming.measure().
  • AfterResponse.run(work) runs work after the response is sent.
  • The JSON helper: JSON.stringify, JSON.bytes and JSON.parse.
  • OpenAPI answers: a route with Can, GuestMiddleware, ValidateSignature, req.authorize(), Gate.authorize() or req.validateSchema() gets the 401, 403 or 422 answer in the docs. A @Response with the same status wins.

Docs: Routing, Rate limiting, Environment

docs.title: Validation and DTOs
docs.text:
• New rules, each as a fluent rule and a DTO annotation: requiredUnless, requiredWithout, requiredWithoutAll, filled, present, prohibited, prohibitedIf, accepted, declined, different, ulid, afterOrEqual and beforeOrEqual, and the field compare rules.
  • @After and @Before take 'today', 'tomorrow', 'yesterday' and the key of another DateTime field.
  • @ExcludeIf and @ExcludeUnless, and .excludeIf() and .excludeUnless() for fluent objects.
  • .bail() stops the other rules of a schema at the first failure.
  • @Dto(trim: true) trims text. @Dto(coerce: true) lets JSON send "18" or "true". @Dto(attributes: {...}) names the fields in messages.
  • DTOs that have no @RequiredIf or @RequiredWith field are faster.

Docs: Validation, Validation rules

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• Auth().logoutOtherDevices(req, password) ends the other sessions of the user. It needs the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag.
  • Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user) keeps the current session after your own password change.
  • Auth().rotateAccessToken() makes a new access token in place of an old one, with an optional grace time. It needs a nullable rotated_at column. dox auth:tokens-table adds it to new tables. For an old table, add it in a new migration.
  • Auth().setAccessTokenAbilities() changes the abilities of a token.
  • AccessTokenAuthDriver(throwOnError: true) sends a token check error to your ExceptionHandler, so the app can answer 503.

Docs: Authentication

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
• Sub-minute tasks: everySecond(), everyFiveSeconds(), everyThirtySeconds() and more.
  • schedule.exec(executable, args: [...]) runs a process with no shell. schedule.command('queue:work') runs a dox command.
  • Output hooks for these tasks: sendOutputTo(), appendOutputTo() and onOutput().
  • Ping hooks: pingBefore(), thenPing(), pingOnSuccess() and pingOnFailure(), and the If forms.
  • dox schedule:clear-cache removes the overlap locks that a crash left behind.

Docs: Scheduler

docs.title: Socket.IO
docs.text:
• Broadcasting, off by default. Turn it on with SocketIoConfig(broadcasting: true). Broadcast.channel() adds rules for private and presence channels. ShouldBroadcast and broadcast(event) send events. Broadcast.routes() adds POST /broadcasting/auth. Broadcast.fake() is for tests.
  • Queued broadcasting with ShouldBroadcastQueued and Broadcast.useQueue(). It does not depend on dox_queue.
  • Whisper: client to client events on private and presence channels, with whisper: true.
  • ServerOptions(allowRequest:) and ServerOptions(maxSessions:).

Docs: Broadcasting, Socket.IO

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
• LogTransport(bothBodies: true) shows the text body and the HTML body.
  • Queued mail lives in dox_mailer now. Mail.queue() and Mail.later() use dox_queue by default. Mail.configure() registers the mail jobs for the worker.

Docs: Mail

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Storage().put(path, contents, exact: true) writes to that exact path.
  • putFile() and putFileAs().
  • copy, move, files, allFiles, directories, deleteDirectory, missing, getVisibility and setVisibility on Storage().
  • Storage().download(path, name: ...) sets the name that the browser saves.
  • Local disk permissions: true makes visibility a file mode. It is off by default and does nothing on Windows.

Docs: File storage

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
• Layouts: @extends, @section and @yield.
  • @stack, @push and @prepend.
  • @csrf and @method('PUT').
  • Your own tags: View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective()).
  • @include('card', {...}) with variables, @includeWhen, @json and @error. Every template has a json() function. A variable named json in your data still wins.
  • More $loop fields: iteration, count, remaining, even, odd, depth and parent.
  • $attributes.except([...]).
  • Options in ViewConfig: strictVariables, stringZeroIsFalse and bladeOutput. All are off by default.
  • A warning for tags that Dox does not have, like @foreach. bladeWarnings: false turns it off.

Docs: Views

docs.title: Inertia
docs.text:
• Inertia.withViewData(req, data) gives values to the root view. {{ csrfToken }} is filled for you.
  • Inertia.setRootView() and RootViewMiddleware use another root view.
  • Server side rendering: ssr: InertiaSsr() in InertiaConfig. If the SSR server is down, the normal page is sent.
  • History encryption with encryptHistory: true, and Inertia.clearHistory(req).

Docs: Inertia

docs.title: OpenAPI, MCP and CLI
docs.text:
• OpenAPI: ApiDoc.route() takes paramResponses. A model visibleFields list is read for the schema.
  • MCP: McpOAuth(now:) takes a fake clock for tests.
  • CLI: dox route:list (and --json), make:provider, make:command, make:mail, make:view and make:test.
  • CLI: make:model takes -m, -c, -r, --api, -f, -s and -a. make:controller takes --resource, --api and --model.

Docs: CLI, Package commands

docs.title: AI skills
docs.text:
Most packages now ship an AI agent skill, like dox-core-guide and dox-orm-guide. skills get finds the packages in your pubspec.yaml, so list dox_cache, dox_validation and dox_openapi there too to get their skills. Install them in your app:

dart run skills@ get --all

A 3.1 app can delete the old .agents/skills/dox folder and the .claude/skills/dox link.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
These are the changes that most apps need to act on.

  • Upgrade the Dox packages together. The new dox_builder finds providers in dox_annotation, so an old dox_builder does not find them. The native drivers changed too, so upgrade dox_postgres_native and dox_mysql_native together with dox_orm.
  • New field names in the JSON logs. In Logger lines, level is now status and name is now logger.name. The values are lower case now (info, warn, danger). In LogMiddleware lines, source_ip is now network.client.ip and request_id is now http.request_id. Check your log parsers and dashboards. LogMiddleware now also follows LoggerConfig: with the logger off, or its level above info, no request lines are written.

  • The database queue moved to its own package. Only apps that use the database queue driver need these steps:

    1. Add the package:

      dart pub add dox_queue_database

    2. Make AppQueueProvider extend DatabaseQueueProvider in place of QueueProvider:

      import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

      Remove the old package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart import if nothing else uses it. If you skip this step, the app still builds and starts. The first dispatch() then fails, so check it by hand.

    3. In your create_queue_tables migration, import package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart.

    4. Only if you want job batches: add a new migration that calls QueueTables.upBatches(schema).

    Mail jobs that are already in a queue keep their names, so they still run.

  • The scheduler process no longer runs queue jobs. In 3.1, bin/schedule.dart also started a queue worker when the in-process worker was on. Now only the web server (QueueConfig(inProcess: true)) or bin/queue.dart runs jobs. If your jobs only ran in the scheduler process, start a worker.

  • maxConnectionAge is a real age now. On MySQL, a connection older than this closes when it is next free, even if it was busy. Before, it was the idle time. Use idleTimeout for the idle time. Postgres now uses this option too.

docs.title: Rare cases
docs.text:
Most apps are not affected by these. Check them if your app does one of these things.

  • A model field with the name of a new query method (skip, sole, reorder, forPage, orderByDesc, updateOrInsert, whereAny, orWhereAny, whereAll, orWhereAll, crossJoin) does not compile. Rename the Dart field and keep the column name with @Column(name: ...). The table does not change:

    @Column(name: 'skip')
int? skipCount;
    - MySQL behind a proxy with its own connection ids, like ProxySQL: a timed out query now gets a KILL, so set serverKill: false. Each new connection also runs one small query to learn the server name. - The job code generator moved to dox_builder. Upgrade dox_builder and dox_queue together. If your build.yaml names dox_queue:jobs, change it to dox_builder:jobs. A plain Dart app needs dart pub add dev:dox_builder. - Nested DTOs deeper in lists and maps are now checked, like List<List<A>>. Such a DTO can now give validation errors. - View text like @json(...) or @error(...) is now a tag. To print it as text, write @@json(...). - RedactedMailError is now imported from package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart. - Queue.fake() no longer catches a custom queue set with Mail.useQueue(). - Custom queue drivers: call Queue.retriedPayload() in place of JobPayload.retried(). - Logger writes in groups, every 20 ms or 64 KB. Warnings and errors are still written at once. - The native HTTP server refuses broken requests that used to pass, like Transfer-Encoding in an HTTP/1.0 request, or a method like GOT that came in as GET. - MCP: the token route answers 401 for invalid_client, not 400. - OpenAPI: operation ids that clashed for optional routes now both use the long form.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Native HTTP: Transfer-Encoding in an HTTP/1.0 request or in two headers is refused. A proxy in front could read the body another way (request smuggling).

docs.title: Routing and core
docs.text:
• Route.group, Route.domain, Route.middleware and the CORS helpers restore their state when the callback throws. Before, the next routes got the wrong path or middleware.
  • Dox().stop() closes the IsolateBus again, so the process can end.
  • Pretty Logger lines for debug, warning and error have a color.

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• orWhere inside whereHas, withCount and preload callbacks no longer matches rows of other parents.
  • When the UPDATE of save() fails, the model stays dirty, so the next save() sends the changes again.
  • chunk() with an orderBy() on a column that is not unique no longer reads a row twice or skips one.
  • transaction(connection: 'main') with the name of the default connection now joins the transaction.
  • insertGetId() drops keys that fillable and guarded do not allow, before it looks for the id.
  • SQLite: a plain query no longer runs inside a transaction that started in the same event-loop turn.
  • Postgres native: a query that times out now gets a CancelRequest. A wrong DataRow is refused. A server error that is not UTF-8 no longer hides the real error. A query in a hand-opened transaction is not sent again after a "cached plan" error.
  • MySQL native: a schema change inside a multi-statement query is seen. -- with no space is not a comment. A backslash is read both ways with NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES. A bad auth switch, a huge column name, a result over 4 GiB, a text that is not UTF-8 and a bad JSON value no longer stop the process or hang the request.
  • Native drivers: each download try of the native library has a 60 second limit.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
• Builder: @OrDefault() on a Maybe<T> field no longer stops the build.
  • Queue: the worker now stops on SIGTERM when Redis is down. A job that a late pop returns is released back to the queue.
  • Auth: after once() or attempt() logs in another user, the access token of the request is dropped. So revokeToken() and tokenCan() use the right user.
  • Mail: an error in an onSent hook no longer fails send() after the email was sent. In a queue worker, it no longer sends the email again.
  • Scheduler: schedule list shows between(), unlessBetween() and environments().
  • Socket.IO: a closed IsolateAdapter no longer piles up listeners, and no longer makes other isolates wait 5 seconds in a shutdown.
  • Storage: copy() and move() of a missing file throw FileNotFoundException and make no folders. size() and lastModified() of a missing file answer 404, not 500. directoryExists('') is true on every disk. storeAs() and putRequestFileAs() return the stored key.
  • Views: text like @empty (none) or @class (see docs) no longer throws. Many nested tags with a space before the ( no longer parse very slowly. Spaces after the last tag are removed.
  • Inertia: an empty 200 that goes back to the page keeps the headers and cookies of the controller.
  • MCP: the token route gives invalid_grant, not 500, when a lock of a code times out. A code now ends exactly after codeTtl.
  • Redis client: one socket failure calls onError once. setSocket() on a connected client uses the new socket.

docs.title: Full list
docs.text:
Every change is in the changelogs:

  • The Changelog page of the docs (dox_core, dox_builder, dox_annotation, dox_cache, dox_cache_database).
  • GitHub releases: dox, dox-orm, dox-auth, dox-validation, dox-mcp, dox-cli, dox-queue, dox-mailer, dox-scheduler, dox-storage, dox-socketio, dox-view, dox-inertia, dox-openapi, dox-http-native, dox-postgres-native and dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: A tour of Dox features
docs.text:
This post is a short tour of the parts that come with Dox, from routing and validation to the ORM, login, queues, mail and the CLI.

Each item has one to three lines and a link to its docs page. Some parts are in the core package dox_core. Other parts are separate packages. You add only the ones you need.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• Routing: Routes for each HTTP method, route params, groups, resource routes and named routes. Signed routes and route model binding are included.
  • Middleware: Class or function middleware for one route, a group, a router or all routes. Request id, ETag and request timeout middleware come with it.
  • Request and response: Read input, headers, files and the client IP. Return a model, a map or a list, and Dox sends JSON. Files and big responses are streamed.
  • DTO validation: Write a @Dto class with rules on its fields. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 answer.
  • OpenAPI: dox_openapi makes OpenAPI 3.1 docs from your routes and DTOs. It also serves a docs page at /docs.
  • Sessions and CSRF: Sessions with a cookie or cache driver, and flash data. CSRF protection for forms.
  • Cookies: Set cookies on a response and read them from a request. Dox encrypts cookies with your APP_KEY.
  • Encryption and hashing: Crypt encrypts and decrypts text with the app key. Hash hashes and checks passwords. Hash.makeAsync and Hash.verifyAsync do not block the server.
  • Rate limiting: The RateLimit middleware stops a client that sends too many requests. With a Redis cache, all servers share the counts.
  • Security headers: The SecurityHeaders middleware sets safe default headers. You can change or turn off each header.
  • CORS: Allow one or more origins, and answer preflight requests.
  • Static files: Serve a folder or a storage disk with one line. You can also serve a single page app.
  • Health checks: A health route for a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes. It can check the database and the cache.
  • IoC container: Add @Inject() to a class, and Dox makes it and its parameters for you. The container is generated code. It does not use reflection.
  • Providers: A provider sets up a package or a service when the app starts, and cleans up when it stops.
  • Exception handler: Every error goes to one handler. It logs the error and decides what the client gets.
  • Logging: The Logger prints colored text in development, or one JSON object per line for a log service.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• ORM models: A model is a class for one table. Save, find, delete, hide fields and mass assignment rules are included.
  • Relations: Has one, has many, belongs to, many to many and polymorphic relations. You can query and count relations too.
  • Scopes and casts: A scope is a query part you use again and again. A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart, like JSON or an enum.
  • Factories and seeders: A factory makes models with sample data for tests. A seeder puts data in your database.
  • Migrations: Write the schema in Dart, then run, roll back or check migrations with the CLI.
  • Query builder and transactions: Build SQL from chained methods with bound values. Run many queries in one transaction.
  • Databases: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• Guards: Use more than one guard in one app, or write your own, like an API key guard.
  • JWT: dox_auth logs users in with JWT tokens. Tokens can be revoked.
  • Session login: Log users in with a session cookie for web pages.
  • Access tokens: Tokens saved in the database, with abilities. You can revoke them one by one.
  • Gates and policies: A gate checks one action. A policy groups the checks for one model. Use them in a controller or on a route.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
• Cache: dox_cache comes with dox_core, so there is nothing to add. It has memory, file and Redis stores, with tags and locks.
  • Queue: dox_queue runs slow work in the background. It has Redis, database and sync drivers, retries, delays and a worker.
  • Scheduler: dox_scheduler runs tasks on a schedule, like cron. You write the schedule in Dart.
  • Mail and notifications: dox_mailer sends email with SMTP, Amazon SES, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark and more. A notification can go out on more than one channel.
  • Storage: dox_storage gives one API for local disk, AWS S3 and S3-compatible services, with signed URLs.
  • Socket.IO: dox_socketio is a Socket.IO v4 server. The official clients connect with no changes.
  • Views: dox_view is an HTML template engine. Templates are .dox.html files.
  • Inertia: dox_inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, with routes and controllers in Dox.
  • MCP: dox_mcp serves tools to MCP clients from a normal Dox route. Tool arguments are checked before your code runs.
  • Redis: Redis is not a separate package to install. It is a driver in the cache, the queue and the Socket.IO adapter. These packages bring their own Redis client. Use Redis when you run more than one server.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• CLI generators: dox make:controller, make:model, make:dto, make:middleware, make:migration, make:factory, make:seeder, make:job and more.
  • Testing helpers: DoxTestClient runs the app inside a test. It can keep a session and log in as a user.
  • dox build: Builds the app into one native binary. It does not need the Dart SDK.
  • Docker: The project has a Dockerfile and a compose file. The image holds only the binary and the files it needs.
  • App template: dox create starts from this template. It has an AGENTS.md file and a skill with step-by-step recipes for AI coding tools.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: Install the CLI and make your first project: Installation.

docs.title: Dox patch release: 21 November 2026
docs.text:
This release is patch versions only. It adds the MCP protocol 2026-07-28, new route options in dox_core, and fixes in auth, ORM, validation, mail, Socket.IO and Redis. A few fixes refuse input that passed before, so read Read before you update.

HTTP/2, gRPC and GraphQL are also new in this release. They have their own posts: HTTP/2 and gRPC and GraphQL.

Key takeaways

  • MCP 2026-07-28. Old and new MCP clients work on the same route. A tool can ask the user a question during a call.
  • New route options. withoutMiddleware<T>(), renderErrorsWith(), Route.fallback(when:) and req.takeOverResponse().
  • Login fixes. On MySQL, a number in a login field could match the wrong user. This is fixed.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only. Run dart pub upgrade, then check Read before you update.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_core 3.2.4 dox_cache 3.2.2 dox_auth, dox_mcp, dox_mailer, dox_socketio 3.2.2 dox_orm, dox_migration, dox_cache_database 3.2.3 dox_openapi, dox_validation 3.2.1 dox_inertia 3.2.3 dox_http_native 3.2.2 ioredis 3.2.2 dox CLI 3.2.3 App template v3.2.4

No change: dox_annotation, dox_builder, dox_queue, dox_queue_database, dox_scheduler, dox_storage, dox_view, dox_postgres_native and dox_mysql_native.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions:

    dart pub upgrade

  2. Update the CLI:

    dart pub global activate dox

  3. Read Read before you update.

docs.title: MCP 2026-07-28
docs.text:
dox_mcp supports the MCP protocol 2026-07-28, next to the older versions on the same route. Your app code does not change.

  • A 2026-07-28 client needs no initialize and no session.
  • A tool can ask the user a question during a call. Return McpToolResult.inputRequired(...) and read the answer with context.answer(input). Inputs are confirm, text, number, choice, form and url.
  • OAuth client metadata documents (CIMD) are supported, as the new spec asks. POST /oauth/register still works for older clients.
  • The server writes a warning once when allowedOrigins is not set. Without it, any website can call the server from a browser.

docs.title: Route options
docs.text:
• .withoutMiddleware<T>() removes every middleware of type T from a route, also global and group middleware. For example, a long stream can skip a global RequestTimeout.
  • .renderErrorsWith(renderer) sends the errors of a route to your own renderer.
  • Route.fallback(controller, when: check) tries the fallback for any method, and it answers only when the check gives true.
  • req.takeOverResponse() tells Dox that the handler sends the response itself.

docs.title: Other new features
docs.text:
• dox_auth: Ability.viewAny, view, create, update and delete constants for policies.
  • dox_orm: EnumCast(Status.values, unknown: Status.other) gives a value for an unknown stored enum value.
  • dox_inertia: dox inertia:install --ssr writes the React SSR entry, and dox inertia:start-ssr starts the SSR server.
  • dox_openapi: a faster docs build for apps with many routes. 1000 routes took about 2.5 seconds before.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Login on MySQL. A number in a login field, like {"email": 0}, matched almost any user, and the password was checked against the first one. Now the value goes into the query as text.
  • Login on Postgres. A login value that does not fit a number column gave a 500 error. Now it is a failed login.
  • Unknown enum values. One stored enum value that the enum does not have made the whole query fail. Now a nullable field reads it as null, and the ORM logs a warning. Saving the model does not overwrite the stored value.
  • Cache keys. A user key could hit an internal key. For example, forget('lock:report') freed the lock of lock('report').
  • Socket.IO. An event packet with no data threw in the server. A very deep auth value could overflow the stack. A room name in X-Socket-ID made toOthers skip the whole room.
  • Redis subscribers. Four sets of subscriber-mode fixes in ioredis. For example, two subscribe() calls on the same channel now both get the messages, and ping() works in subscriber mode.
  • CLI. seeders.dart and migrations.dart no longer list abstract or sealed classes, so the app compiles.
  • OpenAPI. A : in a route path, like /books:search, shows as it is. It no longer becomes a param.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text:
• Cache keys. User keys that start with lock:, tag:, flexible:created: or # are stored under a new name. They miss the cache one time after the update.
  • Mail addresses. An email address with a character that is not ASCII, like user@münchen.de, now throws a MailException. Write the domain in punycode, like user@xn--mnchen-3ya.de. Display names and subjects can still be any text.
  • Validation. Some input that passed before now fails, because the old result was wrong:
    • Dates and times that do not exist, like 2024-02-31 or 10:61.
    • Infinity in v.num().
    • Hex text like "0x1F" in v.coerce.int() and v.coerce.num().
    • A double above 2^53 in a DTO int field.
  • Socket.IO depth. Text packets are limited to 32 levels, the same as binary packets. Set ServerOptions.maxDepth to change this.
  • OpenAPI. The spec no longer has the x-dox-middleware extension, because it showed internal class names.
  • ioredis. RedisConnection.patternListeners is now Map<String, List<RedisSubscriber>>. Only code that reads this field directly must change.

Full list: the CHANGELOG of each package.

docs.title: Dox patch release: 22 November 2026
docs.text:
This release is patch versions only. It makes the tail latency lower on servers with 4 or more CPU cores, and it makes routes with params faster. One fix changes the match of two rare routes, so read Read before you update.

Key takeaways

  • Lower tail latency. On 4 server cores with 64 connections, p99 goes from 2.4 ms to 0.3 ms.
  • Faster param routes. A route like /users/{id} is matched without a regex. The match goes from 142 ns to 16 ns.
  • Route parts with text and params. Routes like /v{id}/{name} now give each param its own value.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only. Run dart pub upgrade, then check Read before you update.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_core 3.2.5 dox_http_native 3.2.3 dox_grpc 0.0.2

No change: all the other packages, the dox CLI and the app template.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions:

    dart pub upgrade

  2. Build or start the app again. The new native library downloads automatically.

  3. Read Read before you update.

There is no API change and no config change.

docs.title: Lower tail latency on more cores
docs.text:
The HTTP server of Dox runs on native threads, and it gives each request to Dart. Before this release, the server gave its sockets to an idle thread as soon as it sent an answer. Each return to Dart then cost 2 thread wake-ups. On a server with idle CPU cores, these wake-ups made some requests wait.

Now the server waits up to 1 ms for the next requests in the same call, after it sends a whole answer and no request is open.

4 server cores p99 before p99 now 64 connections 2.4 ms 0.3 ms 256 connections 2.8 ms approximately 1 ms

With 64 connections, the server also does 1% to 6% more requests a second. On 2 server cores, the numbers do not change.

There is no wait while a request or a streamed answer is open. A WebSocket message and a part of a streamed answer do not start a wait.

docs.title: Param routes without a regex
docs.text:
A route with params like /users/{id} is now matched without a regex, when each part of its path is plain text or one whole param. The match goes from 142 ns to 16 ns. On 2 server cores, GET /user/{id} does 2% to 4% more requests a second.

Routes with {id?}, {path*} or Route.where use the regex, as before. The matched routes and the param values do not change.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Route parts with text and params. A route part can have text and params together, like /v{id}/{name}, /v{id} and /{a}-{b}. Before, /v{id}/{name} gave the value of id for req.param['name']. Now each param has its own name and value. Route.url also fills the params of such a route.
  • Gzip answers. A gzip answer sometimes did not go out until other traffic came. Now the server sends the answer in the same call.
  • gRPC install. The router file that dox grpc:install writes no longer tells you to keep Route.middleware out. A service can go inside Route.middleware, after the health service.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text:
• Two rare route matches change. Examine your routes for a part that has text and a param together.
    • /v{id} now matches /v5. Before, it matched only the text /v{id}.
    • /{a}-{b} now matches /x-y but not /x. Before, it was one param with the name a}-{b.
  • dox_core 3.2.5 needs dox_http_native 3.2.3. dart pub upgrade gets it.

Full list: the CHANGELOG of each package.

docs.title: Dox patch release: 24 November 2026
docs.text:
This release is patch versions only. Dox has a new native HTTP client, and five packages now send their requests through it. The Linux libraries of the native packages no longer need libgcc_s, so the Docker image of an app is simpler.

Key takeaways

  • New package: dox_http_client. A native HTTP client for Dart, with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. It works in any Dart app.
  • Faster requests to other servers. Mail, S3 storage, Inertia SSR, scheduler pings and the MCP OAuth fetcher use the new client.
  • Simpler Docker image. The Dockerfile of an app does not copy libgcc_s.so.1 any more.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only. Run dart pub upgrade, then check Read before you update.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_http_client 0.0.4 (new) dox_mailer 3.2.3 dox_storage 3.2.3 dox_inertia 3.2.4 dox_scheduler 3.2.3 dox_mcp 3.2.3 dox_http_native 3.2.4 dox_postgres_native 3.2.2 dox_mysql_native 3.2.2 dox_pdf_lib 0.0.4 App template v3.2.5

No change: all the other packages and the dox CLI.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions:

    dart pub upgrade

  2. Build or start the app again. The new native libraries download automatically.

  3. Read Read before you update.

There is no API change and no config change.

docs.title: dox_http_client
docs.text:
dox_http_client is a native HTTP client. Use it when your app calls another server, for example an API in a handler.

import 'package:dox_http_client/dox_http_client.dart';

final DoxHttpClient client = DoxHttpClient();

Future<String> rates() async {
  DoxHttpClientResponse res = await client.get(
    Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/rates'),
  );
  return res.body;
}
  • Rust owns the sockets and reads the answers. The socket work runs on the thread of your isolate, which makes the client faster than HttpClient of dart:io.
  • On https://, the client uses HTTP/2 when the server has it. The requests to one server then share one connection.
  • The client keeps its connections open and uses them again.
  • It follows redirects, decodes gzip and brotli bodies, and streams big bodies with a small memory use.
  • DoxHttpPackageClient is a Client of package:http. Give it to a package that takes an http.Client. It passes all the tests of the Dart team for package:http clients.

The package does not depend on Dox. The version line starts at 0.0.x, so the API can still change.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text:
Five packages now send their requests through dox_http_client:

Package What uses the native client dox_mailer The HTTP transports: Resend, SES, Mailgun, Postmark and Azure dox_storage The S3 driver dox_inertia The request to the SSR server dox_scheduler The pings, like pingBefore and thenPing dox_mcp McpOAuthHttpFetcher, which loads client metadata documents

Mail and S3 requests use HTTP/2 when the server has it. Your code does not change. A client that you pass, like client in a mail transport or httpClient in the S3 driver, is used as before. A custom sendPing of the scheduler is used as before too.

docs.title: Simpler Docker image
docs.text:
Before this release, the Linux libraries of the native packages needed libgcc_s.so.1. A FROM scratch image does not have this file, so the Dockerfile of an app copied it. Without the copy, the app did not start.

Now the ready-built Linux libraries need only glibc 2.34 or newer, as before. This applies to dox_http_native, dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native, dox_pdf_lib and dox_http_client.

A new app from template v3.2.5 has a Dockerfile without the copy. In an app that you already have, you can remove these lines after the update:

  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

Remove the \ at the end of the line before them too. The lines do no harm if you keep them. See the Docker guide for the full file.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text:
• connectTimeout of McpOAuthHttpFetcher has a new meaning. It is now the limit for the lookup of the host only. timeout is the limit for the connection and for the answer. The guards against SSRF do not change.
  • Remove the libgcc_s lines only after the update. With dox_http_native older than 3.2.4, an image without libgcc_s.so.1 stops at start with dox_http_native did not load.
  • New release tags of dox_http_native. The tag is now dox_http_native-v<version>, because the repository holds 2 packages. The build hook finds the library automatically. This is important only if you download the library with your own script.

Full list: the CHANGELOG of each package.

docs.title: Dox patch release: 27 November 2026
docs.text:
This release is patch versions only. Dox can now serve HTTPS with no proxy, and each server isolate can have its own memory. The two features are off by default. The release also has fixes for request bodies that are not valid.

Key takeaways

  • HTTPS without a proxy. Set tls in the app config with a certificate file and a key file. Read HTTPS without a proxy in Dox.
  • Isolate groups. One flag gives each isolate its own heap and its own garbage collector. Read Isolate groups.
  • Fixes for bad request bodies. A multipart body that is not valid now gets a 400. Before, the request could wait with no answer.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only. Run dart pub upgrade, then check Read before you update.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_http_native 3.2.6 dox_core 3.2.6 dox_orm 3.2.4 dox_migration 3.2.4 dox_cache_database 3.2.4 App template v3.2.6

dox_orm and dox_cache_database have no changes. Their version goes up with dox_migration.

No change: all the other packages and the dox CLI.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions:

    dart pub upgrade

  2. Build or start the app again. The new native library downloads automatically.

  3. Read Read before you update.

There is no API change. An app that does not turn on the new features works the same as before.

docs.title: HTTPS without a proxy
docs.text:
Dox can do the TLS work itself. Set tls in the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  serverPort: 443,
  tls: TlsOptions(
    certificatePath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem',
    keyPath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem',
  ),
  // ...
);
  • The server uses TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The TLS work is in Rust, with rustls. There is no OpenSSL.
  • With http2: true, browsers and gRPC clients use HTTP/2 with no proxy.
  • Dox().server.reloadCertificate() uses a new certificate without a restart.
  • req.scheme() is https. Cookies get Secure, and SecurityHeaders sends HSTS.
  • DoxTestClient speaks HTTPS when the config has tls.
  • A new app from template v3.2.6 has the TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY keys. Set them in .env to turn on HTTPS without a code change.

Dox does not get or renew a certificate, and it does not redirect http:// to https://. For these, keep a proxy. See HTTPS without a proxy.

docs.title: Isolate groups
docs.text:
By default, all server isolates share one heap and one garbage collector, and the Dart VM runs only 8 of them at the same time. Turn on isolateGroups to give each isolate its own heap:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  flags: CoreFlags(isolateGroups: env.appEnv == 'production'),
  // ...
);
  • A garbage collection in one isolate does not stop the others.
  • The limit of 8 isolates does not apply.
  • Each isolate runs main() again. Dox().isPrimary is true only in the first isolate. Use it for work that must run one time.
  • With dox_migration 3.2.4, the migrations in main() run only in the first isolate.

See Give each isolate its own memory.

docs.title: A warning for servers with more than 8 CPU cores
docs.text: The Dart VM runs 8 isolates at the same time by default, so a bigger server used only approximately 8 cores. Dox now shows a warning at the start when the app has more isolates than the VM runs. The warning gives the DART_VM_OPTIONS value that lets all isolates run.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Multipart bodies that are not valid. Some bad multipart/form-data bodies made the request wait with no answer, and the server then did not stop on shutdown. Others gave a 500. Now they get a 400.
  • Bracket keys with an unusual index. A key such as k[01]=z or k[+1]=z lost its value in req.body, req.query and a DTO. Now only plain digits are a list index. Other keys are map keys and keep their value: k[01]=z gives {k: {01: z}}.

Fuzz tests found these bugs.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text:
• dox_core 3.2.6 needs dox_http_native 3.2.6. dart pub upgrade gets the two together.
  • The native library is bigger. The library of dox_http_native goes from approximately 0.6 MB to approximately 1.4 MB, because it now has the TLS code.
  • A bracket key that is not plain digits is now a map key. k[01]=z gave a list before, with a lost value. Now it gives a map. A key like k[+5000] got a 422 before. Now it is a map key too.
  • With isolate groups, main() runs in each isolate. Read your settings and the app key from the env, not from command line arguments.

Full list: the CHANGELOG of each package.

docs.title: Dox vs Go: speed and memory
docs.text: In our published benchmark on 2 CPU cores, a Dox app handled 2× to 4.8× the requests per second of a Go app. Go used less memory once a database was added.

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
Requests per second at 256 connections. The last column shows how many times the requests of Go that Dox handled:

Test Dox Go Dox handles Plain HTTP, GET / 638,067 242,043 2.6× Plain HTTP, GET /user/:id 572,658 230,845 2.5× Plain HTTP, POST /user 545,986 231,050 2.4× JSON, GET /json 555,216 206,398 2.7× One row from Postgres, GET /db 266,432 55,903 4.8× 20 rows from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 17,772 6,635 2.7× One row from MySQL, GET /db 247,242 55,322 4.5× 20 rows from MySQL, GET /queries?n=20 12,347 5,520 2.2×

The smallest gap is 2×, on GET / at 64 connections. The JSON row is from the Postgres run.

This post compares Dox with Go only. The full tables also have other servers. You can find them, and the full method, on the Performance page. Every number here comes from that page.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2, with 8 CPUs in the Docker VM (linux/arm64).
  • The server gets 2 CPUs. The load tool (wrk 4.1) runs on other CPUs.
  • One server runs at a time. Connections use keep-alive.
  • Each server has one worker per core. Dox has one isolate per core. Go is one process with GOMAXPROCS=2.
  • Dox is an AOT build (dox build) with Dart 3.13.6. Go is version 1.26.
  • The Go app uses the standard library server, net/http. We did not test other Go servers or frameworks.
  • 5 seconds of warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the whole container.

docs.title: Plain HTTP
docs.text:
The test follows the rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks. Dox is a full Dox app with three routes. Go uses net/http with http.ServeMux.

Requests per second on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxfull app 638,067fastest Gonet/http 242,0432.6× slower

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Peak memory on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Peak memory of the container, lower is better.

peak Doxfull app 19 MBlowest Gonet/http 36 MB1.9× more

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

GET /, requests per second:

Server 64 connections 256 connections 512 connections p99 at 256 peak MB Dox 494,223 638,067 612,032 0.74 ms 19 Go (net/http) 248,951 242,043 232,687 3.27 ms 36

The other two routes, at 256 connections:

Server GET /user/:id POST /user Dox 572,658 545,986 Go 230,845 231,050

Dox handled 2× the requests of Go at 64 connections, and 2.6× at 256 and 512 connections. On the other two routes it handled 2.5× and 2.4×. Its peak memory was 19 MB. Go's peak was 36 MB. Both are small.

docs.title: A small app with a database
docs.text:
This test is closer to a real app:

  • GET /json returns a map as JSON.
  • GET /db reads one row by id.
  • GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows, one after another.

Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native or dox_mysql_native. Go uses pgx or go-sql-driver. The server gets 2 CPUs and the database gets 2 CPUs. Each server has 8 database connections in total. There was one run of 15 seconds per route.

Read one row on 2 cores

GET /db on Postgres 18, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxdox_postgres_native 266,432fastest Gopgx 55,9034.8× slower

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Peak memory with Postgres on 2 cores

256 connections. Peak memory of the container, lower is better.

peak Gopgx 31 MBlowest Doxdox_postgres_native 106 MB3.4× more

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Postgres 18, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_postgres_native) 555,216 266,432 17,772 106 Go (net/http + pgx) 206,398 55,903 6,635 31

MySQL 8.4, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_mysql_native) 558,886 247,242 12,347 70 Go (net/http + go-sql-driver) 211,713 55,322 5,520 27

On /db with Postgres, the p99 was 1.8 ms for Dox and 6.3 ms for Go.

Three things to see here:

  • Dox handled more requests on every route. The gap is largest on /db: 4.8× with Postgres and 4.5× with MySQL.
  • On /json it handled 2.7×. On 20 queries per request it handled 2.7× with Postgres and 2.2× with MySQL.
  • Go used less memory. Its peak was 31 MB with Postgres and 27 MB with MySQL. The peak of Dox was 106 MB and 70 MB.

docs.title: Why the numbers differ
docs.text:
We did not profile the Go app. So we can not say where its time goes. But the two servers are built in different ways:

  • How a request runs. In Dox, the native HTTP server runs on the thread of the isolate. One call writes the answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Under load, no other thread is involved. In Go, net/http starts one goroutine per connection, and the Go scheduler runs the goroutines on the threads.
  • How a query is sent. The Dox drivers send many queries down one connection at once (pipelining). In the Go app, each query takes one connection from the pool and waits for its answer. With 8 connections, at most 8 queries run at the same time.
  • Memory. Both are one process with a compiled binary and no JIT compiler. This helps both stay small on plain HTTP. We did not measure why Dox needs more memory than Go when a database is added.

What makes Dox fast explains the Dox side in more detail.

docs.title: Measure your own app
docs.text:
These numbers come from one machine and very small apps. Your app is different. It has more routes, more data and its own code. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own logic. So the gap in your app can be smaller or larger.

Before you choose, build your app with dox build and measure it on your own server. The Performance page shows how we ran the tests, so you can run them the same way.

docs.title: Dox vs Node.js: memory and speed
docs.text:
In our published benchmark on 2 CPU cores, a Dox app served more requests per second than a Node.js app and used much less memory.

This post compares Dox with Node.js only. The full tables also have other servers. You can find them, and the full method, on the Performance page. Every number here comes from that page.

Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native or dox_mysql_native. Node uses pg or mysql2. The server gets 2 CPUs and the database gets 2 CPUs. Each server has 4 database connections per core, so 8 in total. There was one run of 15 seconds per route.

docs.title: Why Dox uses less memory
docs.text:
We did not measure where each megabyte goes. But these design choices make a difference:

  • One process. Dox runs one process with one isolate per core. The isolates share one compiled program. The Node app runs one process per core plus a primary process, and each one loads its own JavaScript engine and its own copy of the app.
  • No JIT compiler. dox build makes an AOT binary, so no compiler runs next to your app. Node compiles JavaScript while the app runs.
  • Socket work outside the Dart heap. The native HTTP server reads the sockets and parses HTTP in native code.
  • One database pool. All isolates share one pool for the whole process.

What makes Dox fast explains each of these in more detail.
