docs.title: Dox vs Serverpod: which Dart backend fits your app
docs.text:
Dox and Serverpod are both full Dart backends with an ORM and migrations, but Serverpod is built around a Flutter client, and Dox is a plain HTTP API for any client.

Our post Dart backend frameworks: how to choose puts five options in one table. This post looks only at Dox and Serverpod, because they are the two that people compare most when they want a full backend. We show the same tasks in both, with code.

We build Dox, so we are not neutral. Every fact about Serverpod links to its own docs. We checked them on 2026-11-20, on Serverpod 4.1.

In brief

  • Your client is a Flutter app, and you want the client code made for you: pick Serverpod.
  • Your API has many kinds of clients, you want a queue and mail in the box, or you use MySQL: pick Dox.

docs.title: The main difference
docs.text:
The two frameworks start from a different idea.

  • Serverpod makes your server and your Flutter app one project. You write a Dart method on the server. Serverpod generates a client, and the app calls the method like a local function. A new project has three packages: _server, _client and _flutter (How it works).
  • Dox makes a plain HTTP API. You write routes and controllers. Any client can call them: a Flutter app, a web app, or another server. Dox makes an OpenAPI document from your routes, so other teams can see the API and make clients from it.

Most other differences come from this one.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
Dox Serverpod API style HTTP routes and controllers Endpoint methods, called through a generated Dart client Client Any. OpenAPI document made for you. Generated Dart client for Flutter Models Dart classes with @DoxModel YAML files (.spy.yaml) Input checks @Dto classes, 422 on bad input Typed method parameters Databases Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite Postgres 16+, SQLite Migrations Written in Dart, dox migrate Made from model files, serverpod create-migration Background jobs Queue (database or Redis) with retries Future calls, stored in the database Scheduled tasks Scheduler (cron, dailyAt, time zones) Recurring future calls (interval or cron) Auth JWT, sessions, access tokens Email, Google, Apple, Facebook, GitHub, Microsoft, Firebase, passkeys Mail SMTP, SES, Resend, Mailgun and more Sign-in emails on Serverpod Cloud; otherwise your own package Real-time Socket.IO server, raw WebSocket Streaming methods over a WebSocket Hosting You deploy it: binary or Docker Serverpod Cloud, or you deploy it with Docker License MIT BSD-3, except the main serverpod package (SSPL)

Sources for the Serverpod column: endpoints, models, database connection, future calls, auth setup, email sign-in, streaming, deploy, pub.dev.

docs.title: Start a project
docs.text:
Both start with no database to install.

Dox
dart pub global activate dox
dox create team_app
cd team_app
dart pub get
dox s

A new Dox app uses SQLite. The database file is made at the first start.

Serverpod
dart install serverpod_cli
serverpod quickstart team_app
cd team_app
serverpod start

A new Serverpod app runs an embedded Postgres that Serverpod downloads for you (Installation). Serverpod 4 needs Flutter 3.44.4 or later on your machine.

docs.title: Write an endpoint
docs.text:
The example app has projects and tasks. We want one call that makes a task.

In Serverpod, an endpoint is a class with methods. The first parameter is always a Session:

Serverpod
class TaskEndpoint extends Endpoint {
  Future<Task> create(Session session, String title, int projectId) async {
    return await Task.db.insertRow(
      session,
      Task(title: title, projectId: projectId),
    );
  }
}

The Flutter app then calls await client.task.create('Write docs', 1);. You write no HTTP code and no JSON parsing. That is the strongest part of Serverpod.

In Dox, you write a DTO, a controller method and a route:

lib/app/dtos/save_task/save_task.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SaveTask {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  final int projectId;

  const SaveTask({required this.title, required this.projectId});

  static const DtoSchema<SaveTask> schema = $SaveTaskDto;
}
lib/app/http/controllers/task.controller.dart
@Inject()
class TaskController {
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SaveTask body) async {
    Task task = Task()
      ..title = body.title
      ..projectId = body.projectId;
    await task.save();
    return response(task).statusCode(201);
  }
}
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/tasks', (TaskController c) => c.store);

This is more code than Serverpod. In return, you get a normal POST /tasks that any HTTP client can call. Bad input gets a 422 with the errors, and the same DTO goes into the OpenAPI document. For a Flutter app, you can put the DTO in a shared package, so the app checks input with the same rules. See Share code with Flutter.

docs.title: Models and the ORM
docs.text:
Serverpod models are YAML files. Serverpod makes the Dart class from them:

Serverpod: task.spy.yaml
class: Task
table: task
fields:
  title: String
  projectId: int

You query with a generated db object and typed column functions (CRUD):

Serverpod
var tasks = await Task.db.find(
  session,
  where: (t) => t.projectId.equals(1),
  limit: 50,
);

Dox models are Dart classes. You write the fields yourself, and build_runner makes the rest:

lib/app/models/project/project.model.dart
@DoxModel(table: 'projects')
class Project extends ProjectGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Task)
  List<Task> tasks = <Task>[];
}
Dox
List<Task> tasks = await Task().where('project_id', 1).limit(50).get();

Project? project = await Project().preload('tasks').find(1);

Both ORMs have relations, transactions and typed results. Pick by taste: YAML that makes the class (Serverpod), or a Dart class you write (Dox).

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Serverpod makes the migration from your model files. You change a .spy.yaml file and run serverpod create-migration. In development, you press M in the serverpod start terminal. In production, you start the server with --apply-migrations (Migrations).

Dox migrations are Dart files that you write, with up and down:

dox make:migration create_tasks_table
dox migrate
db/migration/2026_11_20_120000_create_tasks_table.dart
class CreateTasksTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('tasks', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('title');
      table.foreignId('project_id').constrained();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('tasks');
  }
}

The Serverpod way is less work, because the schema follows the models. The Dox way gives you full control, and the same file runs on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. See Migration.

docs.title: Background jobs and schedules
docs.text:
Serverpod has future calls. A future call is a method that runs later. It is stored in the database, so it survives a restart:

Serverpod
await pod.futureCalls
    .callWithDelay(const Duration(hours: 1))
    .example
    .doWork();

Recurring future calls take an interval or a cron line. On Serverpod Cloud, future calls need the Growth or Enterprise plan (overview).

Dox has a queue and a scheduler. A job is a class. A worker process runs it, with retries and delays:

lib/app/jobs/send_task_report.dart
@Job()
class SendTaskReport extends DoxJob {
  SendTaskReport({required this.projectId});

  final int projectId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    // build the report and send it
  }
}

await SendTaskReport(projectId: 1).dispatch();

The scheduler runs plain functions on a schedule, with time zones:

lib/config/schedule.dart
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
  s.call('report', () => SendTaskReport(projectId: 1).dispatch()).hourly();
}

Both cover "run this later" and "run this every night". Dox adds a separate worker process, retries, and a Redis driver for apps with many jobs.

docs.title: Auth and mail
docs.text:
Serverpod has more sign-in providers in the box: email, Google, Apple, Facebook, GitHub, Microsoft, Firebase and passkeys (auth setup). It also has the Flutter sign-in widgets. For mail, Serverpod Cloud sends the sign-in emails. When you host it yourself, the docs suggest the mailer package (email setup).

Dox has JWT, sessions and access tokens. Social login and password reset are up to your app. Mail is built in, with SMTP, SES, Resend, Mailgun and more, for any email your app sends.

If social login in a Flutter app is the main need, Serverpod saves you more time. If your app sends many kinds of email, Dox saves you more time.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud, a hosted service. You run serverpod cloud deploy, and it runs your server, database and migrations for you. You can also host it yourself with the Dockerfile in the server package (hosting elsewhere).

Dox has no hosted service. dox build makes a native binary, and you run it on a VPS or in Docker. The docs have guides for Docker, a VPS, Fly.io and Cloud Run.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
We did not run this benchmark. The numbers come from the public Web Frameworks Benchmark by the-benchmarker.

Serverpod itself is not in that benchmark. Relic is in it. Relic is the HTTP server from the Serverpod team, and Serverpod's web server is built on it. So this compares the HTTP layer of the two projects. It does not measure Serverpod endpoint calls or a database.

Connections Dox (requests per second) Relic (requests per second) 64 157,805 45,785 256 189,869 45,034 512 189,851 44,291

At 64 connections, half of the Dox requests took 0.11 ms or less. For Relic, it was 0.86 ms.

How they measured it:

  • Three small routes: GET /, GET /user/:id and POST /user.
  • One machine with an AMD Ryzen 7 5700U. The server and the load tool run on it, with the same limits for every framework.
  • Both apps are AOT builds, and both start one isolate per CPU that Dart reports.
  • Versions: dox_core 3.2 and relic 2.0. Results from 2026-11-18. See the raw data and the code of the Dox app and the Relic app.

Small routes show the cost of the framework itself. In a real app, the database and your own code often take most of the time. For how Dox gets these numbers, see What makes Dox fast.

docs.title: When to pick Serverpod
docs.text:
• Your only client is a Flutter app, and you want the client made for you.
  • You want many social sign-in providers and the Flutter sign-in widgets.
  • You want a hosted service, so you do not run servers yourself.
  • You want a project with many years of use. Serverpod has been on pub.dev for about five years.

docs.title: When to pick Dox
docs.text:
• Your API has more than one kind of client, like a web app, a mobile app or other servers.
  • You want an OpenAPI document made from your code.
  • You use MySQL or MariaDB.
  • You want a job queue with a worker, a scheduler and mail in one framework.
  • You want a fast HTTP layer. See Speed.
  • The license matters to you. Dox uses the MIT license.

docs.title: When not to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want the Dart client made for you. Dox does not generate one.
  • You want a hosted service. You deploy Dox yourself.

More gaps are on What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: Can a non-Flutter client call a Serverpod server?
docs.text: Serverpod's docs show the generated Dart client. For plain REST routes, Serverpod has a separate web server, built on Relic, where you add routes by hand. In Dox, every route is plain HTTP, so any client can call it.

docs.title: Can I share models between Flutter and Dox?
docs.text: Yes. Put the @Dto classes in a plain Dart package that the app and the server both use. See Share code with Flutter.

docs.title: Can I move from Serverpod to Dox?
docs.text: Yes, but it is a rewrite of the server code. Your Postgres data can stay. You turn each .spy.yaml model into a @DoxModel class, each endpoint method into a route and a controller method, and each future call into a job. The Flutter app then calls HTTP routes instead of the generated client.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Both are full Dart backends with an ORM and migrations.
  • Serverpod is the better fit for a Flutter-only app that wants the client made for it, and for a hosted service.
  • Dox is the better fit for a plain HTTP API with many clients, MySQL, or a queue and mail in the box.

Want to try Dox? The tutorial builds a small API with a database, validation, login and tests. If you find a wrong fact about Serverpod here, open a GitHub issue, and we will fix it.

docs.title: A full-stack app with Dox and Inertia
docs.text:
This post shows how to build a React app on top of Dox with Inertia, with no separate API between them.

A normal single page app needs two parts: an API on the server and a client that calls it. You write the routes twice, the types twice and the error handling twice.

Inertia removes the API part. A Dox controller gives a page name and its props. Inertia shows that page in the browser, as a React, Vue or Svelte component. The first visit gets a full HTML page. After that, links and forms get only JSON, and the page changes with no reload.

The example is a small team task list. It lists tasks, adds a task with a form, and deletes a task. It uses React, but Vue and Svelte work the same way.

docs.title: The steps in short
docs.text:
1. dart pub add dox_inertia and the npm packages.
  2. resources/views/app.html: the HTML page of the first visit.
  3. lib/config/inertia.dart and a provider.
  4. vite.config.js and resources/js/app.jsx.
  5. Three middleware on the web router.
  6. A controller that renders pages.
  7. A React page with a form.
  8. Run it in dev, then build it for production.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Start from a new Dox app (dox create tasks), then add the server package:

dart pub add dox_inertia

And the client packages:

npm install @inertiajs/react react react-dom
npm install -D vite @vitejs/plugin-react

dox_inertia works with the Inertia 3 client.

docs.title: 2. The root view
docs.text:
The root view is the HTML page of the first visit. It is plain HTML, with no template engine. Dox puts the script and style tags in place of @vite, and the page in place of @inertia.

resources/views/app.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Tasks</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 3. Config and provider
4. Vite and the client entry
5. Middleware
docs.text:
Inertia needs three middleware, in this order:

  • SessionMiddleware: keeps the validation errors and flash messages between requests.
  • CsrfMiddleware: stops form posts from other sites. The Inertia client sends the token by itself, so you write no code for it.
  • InertiaMiddleware: reads the Inertia headers and adds the shared props.

Add them to the web router only. Your /api routes stay as they are.

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:tasks/app/http/controllers/task.controller.dart';
import 'package:tasks/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
    HandleInertiaRequests(),
  ];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/tasks', (TaskController c) => c.index);
    Route.post('/tasks', (TaskController c) => c.store);
    Route.delete('/tasks/{id}', (TaskController c) => c.destroy);
  }
}

Shared props go to every page, like the app name or the signed in user:

lib/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

class HandleInertiaRequests extends InertiaMiddleware {
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> share(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'appName': 'Tasks',
      'auth': () => req.auth?.toJson(),
    };
  }
}

A prop can be a function. It runs only when the prop is sent.

docs.title: 6. The controller
docs.text:
Make a model, a migration and a DTO first:

dox make:model Task -m
dox make:dto SaveTask

Add a title column to the migration, and the same field to the model:

lib/app/models/task/task.model.dart
@DoxModel(table: 'tasks')
class Task extends TaskGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;
}

The DTO checks the form input:

lib/app/dtos/save_task/save_task.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SaveTask {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 120)
  final String title;

  const SaveTask({required this.title});

  static const DtoSchema<SaveTask> schema = $SaveTaskDto;
}

Add dtos: dtos from generated/dtos.g.dart to AppConfig, so the app knows the DTOs.

Now the controller. inertia() takes the request, the page name and the props:

lib/app/http/controllers/task.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:tasks/app/dtos/save_task/save_task.dto.dart';
import 'package:tasks/app/models/task/task.model.dart';

@Inject()
class TaskController {
  Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
    return inertia(req, 'Tasks/Index', <String, dynamic>{
      'tasks': () => Task().all(),
    });
  }

  Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req, SaveTask body) async {
    Task task = Task()..title = body.title;
    await task.save();
    Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'Task added');
    return redirect('/tasks');
  }

  Future<DoxResponse> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
    await Task().where('id', id).delete();
    Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'Task deleted');
    return redirect('/tasks');
  }
}

There is no JSON API here, and no fetch code in the client. Three things happen for you:

  • Validation errors. When the DTO check fails, Dox saves the errors in the session and sends the browser back. The page gets them in the errors prop.
  • Redirects. After a DELETE, the browser must follow the redirect with GET. InertiaMiddleware changes the 302 to a 303 for you.
  • Flash messages. Inertia.flash puts a message in the next page, once.

docs.title: 7. The React page
8. Run it
docs.text:
In dev, run two processes:

dox s

npx vite

Open http://localhost:3000/tasks. Change the React page and it updates at once. Change a Dart file and the server restarts.

For production, build the client:

npx vite build

The files go to public/build. Serve them with a route in register(), or let nginx or Caddy serve the folder:

lib/routes/web.dart
// needs import 'dart:io';
Route.get('/build/{path*}', (String path) {
  if (path.contains('..')) throw NotFoundHttpException();
  // the file names have a hash, so the browser can keep them for a year
  return response(File('public/build/$path')).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
});

When you deploy new assets, the asset version changes. A browser with the old version loads the whole page again, with the new files. You do not need to do anything for this.

docs.title: More you can do
docs.text:
The task list is small, but the same package covers bigger apps:

  • Partial reloads. router.reload({ only: ['tasks'] }) asks for one prop. The other props do not run.
  • Deferred props. Inertia.defer(() => Stats.load()) sends a slow prop right after the first page, so the page shows sooner.
  • Infinite scroll. Inertia.merge(posts) adds new items to the old list.
  • History encryption. Inertia.clearHistory(req) on logout, so the back button can not show private pages.
  • Server side rendering. Turn on InertiaSsr() for full HTML on the first visit, for search engines.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• One app: Dox routes and controllers, React pages.
  • No API layer, no fetch code and no client side router.
  • Validation errors, flash messages and CSRF work with no extra code.
  • Your /api routes still work for mobile apps and other clients.

Full docs: Inertia

docs.title: GraphQL in Dox
docs.text:
The new dox_graphql package makes a GraphQL API for your app from your models. You add annotations to a model, run the builder, and the API is ready.

Key takeaways

  • An API from your models. One annotation adds one query or one mutation. An operation with no annotation does not exist.
  • No N+1 queries. Dox loads a relation for all rows with one database query.
  • Your policies protect the API. can: asks the policy of the model before an operation runs. guard: true needs a login.
  • Safe in production. GraphiQL, introspection and error details are off in production. Limits stop very large queries.
  • Made at build time. The builder makes the schema from your models when you run build_runner.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Run the setup command in your app:

dox add graphql

The command adds the packages, lib/config/graphql.dart and the GraphQL provider. It does not overwrite a file. For an app with no models, use dox add graphql --no-orm.

docs.title: Add a model to the API
docs.text:
Put @GraphQL() on a model. Then add one annotation for each operation that a client can use:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}

@GraphQLAll() adds the posts query, and @GraphQLFind() adds the post query. The id, the columns and the relations of the model are fields that a client can ask for. The fields in the hidden list of the model are never visible, so a password stays on the server.

Run the builder:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Run a query
docs.text:
In development, open http://localhost:3000/graphql in a browser. This URL shows GraphiQL, a page where you write and run queries:

{
  posts(limit: 10) {
    title
    user { name }
  }
}

The result has the same shape as the query:

{ "data": { "posts": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL", "user": { "name": "Ada" } }] } }

Dox loads the users of all ten posts with one database query.

docs.title: All operations
Protect the API
docs.text:
Set guard: true on an operation that a guest must not use. Give an ability with can:, and Dox asks the policy of the model before the operation runs:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
  • filter: hides the rows that the user can not see.
  • owner: 'userId' sets the owner of a new row to the logged-in user.
  • A denied guest gets UNAUTHENTICATED, and a denied user gets FORBIDDEN. The other fields of the request still give their data.

Policies need dox_auth 3.2.2 or newer.

docs.title: Safe in production
docs.text:
In production, GraphiQL and introspection are off, and error details stay on the server. You do not set anything for this.

Limits stop a very large query before it causes much work on your server. For example, a query can nest 64 levels (maxDepth) and load 100,000 values (maxNodes). Set lower values in GraphQLConfig when your API is open to the public.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package Version dox_graphql 0.0.1 (new) dox_graphql_builder 0.0.1 (new) dox_graphql_orm 0.0.1 (new)

The GraphQL packages have their own version line, because they are new.

For more, read GraphQL.

docs.title: HTTP/2 and gRPC in Dox
docs.text:
Dox now serves HTTP/2 and gRPC on the same port as your HTTP routes. HTTP/2 is off by default, so an app that does not turn it on works the same as before.

Key takeaways

  • HTTP/2 on the same port. Set http2: true. The port then accepts HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. Your routes, middleware and controllers do not change.
  • gRPC with the new dox_grpc package. Run dox add grpc, write a .proto file, and register your service with one line.
  • Your middleware runs before each gRPC call. Your HTTP routes and your gRPC services can use the same auth.
  • Fast. On one core, dox_grpc does 48,700 small calls a second. grpc-go does 44,000 and package:grpc does 35,300.
  • Safe by default. Flood limits stop the known HTTP/2 attacks, for example Rapid Reset.

docs.title: Turn on HTTP/2
docs.text:
Set http2 to true in the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  // ...
);

Dox finds the protocol of each connection. Old clients and health checks continue to use HTTP/1.1 on the same port.

A new app from dox create has an APP_HTTP2 key. Set APP_HTTP2=true in .env to turn on HTTP/2 without a code change.

Dox uses h2c: HTTP/2 over plain TCP. Your proxy (for example Caddy or nginx) does the TLS, and then sends the requests to Dox:

browser  --HTTP/2 + TLS-->  proxy  --h2c or HTTP/1.1-->  Dox

For more, read HTTP/2.

docs.title: Serve gRPC
docs.text:
gRPC lets your services call each other with typed messages. You write the calls one time in a .proto file, and each side gets typed code from it.

Run the setup command in your app:

dox add grpc

The command adds the packages, a sample protos/greeter.proto and a gRPC router with the health service. It does not overwrite a file.

Extend the class that protoc makes. Each rpc in the .proto file is one method:

lib/app/grpc/greeter_service.dart
class GreeterService extends GreeterServiceBase {
  @override
  Future<HelloReply> sayHello(ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
    return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
  }
}

Register the service in a router that has no prefix:

lib/routes/grpc.dart
class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()];

  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(GreeterService());
  }
}

The middleware of the router runs before each call. A client sends its token as metadata, and the middleware reads it the same as an HTTP header. When the middleware throws 401, the client gets UNAUTHENTICATED.

dox_grpc supports:

  • The four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming.
  • Deadlines, cancel and metadata.
  • GrpcStatus errors with status details.
  • gzip and message size limits (4 MiB by default).
  • The standard health service.

For more, read gRPC.

docs.title: Tested with real gRPC tools
docs.text: A gRPC server must work with clients in other languages. CI runs the grpc-go interop test suite against dox_grpc three times: direct, behind nginx and behind Caddy. CI also does a test with grpcurl. The HTTP/2 server must pass the strict h2spec conformance suite.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
Calls a second on one core:

Test dox_grpc package:grpc grpc-go Unary, small message 48,700 35,300 44,000 Unary, 100 KB reply 14,600 11,400 17,200 Server streaming, 100 messages of 1 KB 4,390 2,010 6,240

Dox does the most small calls, and small calls are the most usual type of gRPC call. With large messages and with streaming, grpc-go is faster on one core. dox_grpc is faster than package:grpc in all three tests.

On four cores, Dox and grpc-go are almost equal. For the full numbers and the test setup, read the gRPC benchmark.

docs.title: Safe by default
docs.text:
HTTP/2 has its own attacks. A client can open and reset streams very fast, or send many small frames. Dox has limits for these attacks:

  • Too many stream resets (Rapid Reset, CVE-2023-44487 and CVE-2025-8671). The connection first drains: open requests get their answers, and a proxy sends new requests on a new connection. If the resets continue, the connection closes.
  • Too many SETTINGS, PING or empty frames close the connection.
  • A connection has a maximum of 250 open requests (maxConcurrentStreams).
  • Data that waits for a slow reader has a limit for each connection.
  • A gRPC call with no message for 5 minutes ends with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Set idleTimeout to change this.

You do not set anything for these limits. The defaults are correct for most apps.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_grpc 0.0.1 (new) dox_http_native 3.2.2 dox_core 3.2.4 App template v3.2.4

dox_grpc has its own version line, because it is a new package.

To update an app, run dart pub upgrade. HTTP/2 stays off until you turn it on.

docs.title: HTTPS without a proxy in Dox
docs.text:
Dox can now serve HTTPS itself. Give it a certificate file and a key file, and a small server needs no proxy for TLS. HTTPS is off by default, so an app that does not turn it on works the same as before.

Key takeaways

  • Two lines of config. Set tls in the app config with the certificate file and the key file.
  • HTTP/2 for browsers and gRPC, with no proxy. With http2: true, the client selects HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 in the TLS handshake.
  • New certificate without a restart. Call reloadCertificate() after certbot renews the certificate.
  • No OpenSSL. The TLS work is in Rust, with rustls.
  • Fixes for bad request bodies. A multipart body that is not valid now gets a 400. Before, the request could wait with no answer.

docs.title: Turn on HTTPS
docs.text:
Set tls in the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  serverPort: 443,
  tls: TlsOptions(
    certificatePath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem',
    keyPath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem',
  ),
  // ...
);

The two files are PEM files, for example fullchain.pem and privkey.pem of certbot. The server uses TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

Your routes stay the same. WebSocket (wss://) and streamed responses work on the HTTPS port. If a file is bad, the app stops at the start with a clear error.

A new app from dox create has the TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY keys. Set them in .env to turn on HTTPS without a code change:

.env
TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem
TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem

docs.title: Your app knows that it is on HTTPS
docs.text:
With tls, req.scheme() is https and req.isSecure() is true. Dox then does the correct thing for you:

  • The session cookie and other cookies get Secure.
  • SecurityHeaders sends HSTS.
  • req.fullUrl() starts with https://.

docs.title: HTTP/2 and gRPC over TLS
docs.text:
Browsers use HTTP/2 only with TLS. Set http2: true together with tls:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  tls: TlsOptions(certificatePath: 'fullchain.pem', keyPath: 'privkey.pem'),
  // ...
);

Browsers and gRPC clients then use HTTP/2 with no proxy. Old clients continue to use HTTP/1.1 on the same port. grpcurl works without -plaintext.

docs.title: Use a new certificate without a restart
docs.text:
A certificate has an end date, and a tool such as certbot writes a new one before that date. Call reloadCertificate() to use the new certificate:

await Dox().server.reloadCertificate();

New connections get the new certificate, and open connections stay open. If a file is bad, the method throws a TlsException and the server keeps the old certificate.

Your app decides when to call the method. This example calls it when the process gets SIGHUP:

bin/server.dart
Future<void> main() async {
  // ...
  await Dox().startServer();
  ProcessSignal.sighup.watch().listen(reloadCertificate);
}

Future<void> reloadCertificate(ProcessSignal signal) async {
  try {
    await Dox().server.reloadCertificate();
    Logger.info('The server has the new certificate');
  } on TlsException catch (error) {
    Logger.danger('The server keeps the old certificate: $error');
  }
}

Then let certbot send the signal after each renewal:

certbot renew --deploy-hook "systemctl kill --signal=HUP dox"

docs.title: When to keep the proxy
docs.text:
Dox does the TLS, but it does not do everything a proxy does. Keep a proxy such as Caddy or nginx when you need one of these:

  • Automatic certificates. Dox does not get or renew a certificate.
  • A redirect from http:// to https://.
  • More than one app or domain on one server. One port has one certificate.
  • Client certificates (mTLS).

For the full guide, read HTTPS without a proxy.

docs.title: Fixes in this release
docs.text:
• Multipart bodies that are not valid. Some bad multipart/form-data bodies made the request wait with no answer, and the server then did not stop on shutdown. Others gave a 500. Now they get a 400.
  • Bracket keys with an unusual index. A key such as k[01]=z or k[+1]=z lost its value in req.body, req.query and a DTO. Now only plain digits are a list index. Other keys are map keys and keep their value.
  • A warning for servers with more than 8 CPU cores. The Dart VM runs 8 isolates at the same time by default, so a bigger server used only approximately 8 cores. Dox now shows a warning at the start, with the setting that lets all isolates run. See Deployment.

Fuzz tests found the first two bugs.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_http_native 3.2.6 dox_core 3.2.6 App template v3.2.6

To update an app, run dart pub upgrade. HTTPS stays off until you turn it on.

docs.title: Isolate groups: each isolate gets its own memory
docs.text:
Dox can now give each server isolate its own heap and its own garbage collector. One flag turns it on. In our test, the same app did 9% more requests a second, and 18% more with three settings of the Dart VM. The flag is off by default, so an app that does not turn it on works the same as before.

Key takeaways

  • One flag. Set CoreFlags(isolateGroups: true) in the app config.
  • A garbage collection in one isolate does not stop the others. Each isolate has its own heap.
  • No limit of 8 isolates. By default, the Dart VM runs only 8 isolates of one group at the same time.
  • More requests and a lower P99. GET /json on 4 server cores: 9% more requests a second, and a P99 of 4.55 ms, down from 6.35 ms.
  • main() runs in each isolate. Use Dox().isPrimary for work that must run only one time.

docs.title: Why isolates shared memory
docs.text:
Dox runs one isolate for each CPU core. Until now, all these isolates were in one isolate group of the Dart VM. One group has one heap and one garbage collector. This has two effects:

  • When the garbage collector moves objects, all isolates of the group wait.
  • The VM runs a maximum of 8 isolates of one group at the same time. A server with more than 8 CPU cores used only approximately 8 of them.

With isolate groups, each isolate is in its own group. Thus each isolate has its own heap, and a pause in one isolate does not stop the others. The limit of 8 does not apply.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
Set the flag in the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  appKey: env.appKey,
  flags: CoreFlags(isolateGroups: env.appEnv == 'production'),
  // ...
);

Turn it on only in production. In development, the app starts slower and uses more memory with this flag, and one group is sufficient there.

CoreFlags.all() does not turn on this flag.

docs.title: What changes for your app
docs.text:
Each isolate now runs main() of bin/server.dart from the start. Most apps need no change:

  • Migrations. The first isolate runs them before the other isolates start. The other isolates find none to run.
  • Work that must run one time. Put it behind Dox().isPrimary. It is true only in the first isolate.
  • Settings. Each isolate builds the config again. Read your settings and the app key from the env, not from command line arguments.
bin/server.dart
if (Dox().isPrimary) {
  await warmUpReports();
}

IsolateBus, the rate limit and Dox().compute continue to work. Dox().compute has one pool of workers in each isolate.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
On Linux, the bundle of dox build works with no change. On macOS, also make a snapshot file with the name of the executable and .aot:

dart compile aot-snapshot bin/server.dart -o build/bundle/bin/server.aot

If Dox finds no file to start, it prints one warning and the isolates share memory, as before.

docs.title: Give each isolate more memory
docs.text:
The Dart VM keeps free memory pages for one isolate only. To keep them for all isolates, set 32 MB for each isolate:

# 4 isolates: 4 x 32 = 128
ENV DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=128,--new_gen_semi_initial_size=32,--new_gen_garbage_threshold=0

The app is faster and uses more memory, approximately 30 MB for each isolate.

docs.title: What we measured
docs.text:
We ran the same Docker image with the flag off and with the flag on. The server had 4 CPU cores. The load was GET /json (50 objects) with wrk and 256 connections for 15 seconds. Each number is the median of 3 rounds.

Requests a second P50 P99 Memory Flag off 137,253 1.75 ms 6.35 ms 25 MB Flag on 149,925 1.59 ms 4.55 ms 28 MB Flag on, with the VM settings 161,745 1.51 ms 3.16 ms 139 MB

With 2 server cores, the result was almost the same: 9% more requests a second with the flag, and 18% more with the VM settings.

Three limits of this test:

  • The test ran on Linux in Docker on a Mac with 8 cores. Your numbers will be different.
  • A route with an empty body (GET /) got only 1% to 3% more. It makes little garbage, so the garbage collector has little work.
  • We did not measure a server with more than 8 cores.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Turn on the flag when one of these is true:

  • Your server has more than 8 CPU cores.
  • Your routes make many objects, for example big JSON responses.
  • A low P99 is important for your app.

Keep it off for a small server with little memory. The default continues to work, and Dox shows a warning at the start if the app has more isolates than the VM runs.

For the full guide, read Give each isolate its own memory.

docs.text:

To update an app, run dart pub upgrade. Isolate groups stay off until you turn them on.

docs.title: Live updates with Socket.IO in Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to add live updates to a Dox app with Socket.IO. When one user changes data, the screens of the other users change too, with no refresh.

The example is a team app. Many people work in one project. When one member adds a task, the other members should see it at once, with no refresh.

dox_socketio is a Socket.IO v4 server. The official socket.io-client connects to it with no changes. It runs on the same port as your HTTP routes, at /socket.io/.

docs.title: The steps in short
docs.text:
It is four small files on the server and one on the client:

  1. dart pub add dox_socketio
  2. lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart: starts Socket.IO. Three lines.
  3. lib/config/socketio.dart: websocket only, your own sites only.
  4. lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart: signs in the user and joins their room.
  5. lib/app/services/live.service.dart: sends a changed event after a write.
  6. src/lib/live.ts: the client connects and loads the data again on each event.

Many isolates work with no extra setup and no Redis. The rest of this post goes through each step.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
• Each user signs in to the socket with the same token the app already uses for the API.
  • Each socket joins a room for its user: user:<id>.
  • After a write, the server sends a small changed event to the users who can see that data.
  • The event holds only a topic, like tasks. It never holds the data.
  • The app gets the event and loads that data again through the normal API.

Why no data in the event? The API already checks who may see what. If the event only says "tasks changed", those checks stay in one place. A bug in the socket code can not leak data.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
dart pub add dox_socketio

npm install socket.io-client

docs.title: 2. The provider
docs.text:
The provider starts Socket.IO in every isolate. Make the file lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart. It must be in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/socketio.dart';

class AppSocketIoProvider extends SocketIoProvider {
  AppSocketIoProvider() : super(socketIoConfig);
}

docs.title: 3. The config
docs.text:
Make the file lib/config/socketio.dart:

lib/config/socketio.dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/socket/live.namespace.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/settings.dart';

SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  options: ServerOptions(
    transports: const <String>['websocket'],
    allowedOrigins: <String>[settings.appUrl, ...settings.frontendUrls],
  ),
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[LiveNamespace()],
);

Two settings matter here:

  • transports: ['websocket']. Dox runs one isolate per CPU core. One websocket stays on one isolate. Long-polling sends many HTTP requests, and they can reach different isolates. So allow websocket only.
  • allowedOrigins. Only your own pages may open a socket. Other websites get 403.

docs.title: 4. Sign in the socket
docs.text:
Socket.IO gets its requests before the router, so your route auth middleware does not run. Use SocketAuth as a namespace middleware instead. Your function gets the handshake and returns the user, or null.

Make the file lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart:

lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/live.service.dart';

class LiveNamespace extends NamespaceHandler {
  @override
  String get path => '/';

  @override
  List<Middleware> get middleware => <Middleware>[SocketAuth(findUser).handle];

  /// The same checks as the API auth middleware.
  static Future<User?> findUser(Handshake handshake) async {
    String? token = handshake.token;
    if (token == null || token.isEmpty) return null;
    return Dox().ioc.get<UserService>().findByToken(token);
  }

  @override
  void onConnection(Socket socket) {
    User user = socket.user! as User;
    socket.join(LiveService.roomOf(user.id!));
  }
}
  • handshake.token is auth.token from the client.
  • With null, the client gets a connect_error with Unauthorized, and onConnection does not run.
  • The token is checked once, when the socket connects.

findUser can check any token your API already uses. With dox_auth, use Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token). See Log in a socket.

docs.title: 5. Send events after a write
docs.text:
A small service sends the events. SocketIoProvider.server is the Socket.IO server of this isolate.

Make the file lib/app/services/live.service.dart:

lib/app/services/live.service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

@Inject()
class LiveService {
  LiveService(this.projectMembers);

  final ProjectMemberRepository projectMembers;

  static String roomOf(int userId) => 'user:$userId';

  /// Data of [projectId] changed: tell its members.
  Future<void> projectChanged(int projectId, String topic) async {
    try {
      Set<int> users = await projectMembers.userIdsOf(projectId);
      await _emit(users, <String, Object>{'topic': topic, 'projectId': projectId});
    } catch (error) {
      Logger.warn('[live] project $projectId $topic: $error');
    }
  }

  /// Something everyone sees changed, like a notice for all users.
  Future<void> everyoneChanged(String topic) async {
    await SocketIoProvider.server?.emit('changed', <String, Object>{'topic': topic});
  }

  Future<void> _emit(Set<int> users, Map<String, Object> data) async {
    SocketIoServer? io = SocketIoProvider.server;
    if (io == null || users.isEmpty) return;
    BroadcastOperator to = io.to(roomOf(users.first));
    for (int user in users.skip(1)) {
      to = to.to(roomOf(user));
    }
    await to.emit('changed', data);
  }
}

Then call it from your services, after the write. For example, in lib/app/services/task.service.dart:

lib/app/services/task.service.dart
Future<Task> create(int projectId, Map<String, dynamic> data) async {
  Task task = await tasks.create(projectId, data);
  await live.projectChanged(projectId, 'tasks');
  return task;
}
  • A failed send is logged. It never fails the write.
  • to(a).to(b) sends one event to many rooms. A user in two rooms gets it once.
  • Put the calls in services, not controllers. Then queue jobs, scheduled jobs and other entry points send events too.

docs.title: 6. Many isolates, no Redis
docs.text:
Each isolate has its own Socket.IO server, and a client is connected to one of them. So an event sent from isolate 1 must also reach clients on isolate 3.

You do not need to do anything for this. With many isolates, the provider uses the IsolateAdapter. It sends each broadcast to the other isolates of the process. You need no Redis.

With more than one server process, use the Redis adapter.

docs.title: 7. The client
docs.text:
In the frontend, make the file src/lib/live.ts:

src/lib/live.ts
import { io, type Socket } from 'socket.io-client'

let socket: Socket | null = null
let connectedOnce = false

/** Call after sign-in. */
export function startLive() {
  if (socket) return
  socket = io(window.location.origin, {
    transports: ['websocket'],
    auth: sendToken,
  })
  socket.on('connect', onConnect)
  socket.on('changed', onChanged)
}

/** Call on sign-out. */
export function stopLive() {
  socket?.disconnect()
  socket = null
  connectedOnce = false
}

/** A fresh token on every connect and reconnect. */
async function sendToken(done: (data: object) => void) {
  done({ token: (await getToken()) ?? '' })
}

/** Events sent while we were offline are lost, so a reconnect loads all. */
function onConnect() {
  if (connectedOnce) reloadAll()
  connectedOnce = true
}

function onChanged(change: { topic: string; projectId?: number }) {
  if (change.topic === 'tasks' && change.projectId === activeProjectId()) {
    reloadTasks()
  }
  // ... one line per topic
}

Three things to note:

  • auth is a function, not an object. The client calls it on each reconnect, so a token that expired is replaced.
  • Socket.IO does not keep events for a client that is offline. On reconnect, load everything again.
  • transports: ['websocket'] must match the server.

docs.title: 8. The dev proxy
docs.text:
If your frontend dev server proxies the API, add /socket.io with websocket support. With Vite, add it to vite.config.ts:

vite.config.ts
server: {
  proxy: {
    '/api': 'http://localhost:3000',
    '/socket.io': { target: 'http://localhost:3000', ws: true },
  },
},

Without ws: true, the socket can not connect in dev.

docs.title: 9. Test it
docs.text:
You can test it with the real client, from Dart, with the socket_io_client package. A good set of tests:

  • A bad token is refused.
  • A new task reaches the project members, and not a user outside the project.
  • A user who is not signed in gets no events.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Live screens for every user, with no refresh.
  • No data in the events, so the API access checks stay in one place.
  • It works on every isolate, with no Redis.
  • The standard socket.io-client works with no changes.

Full docs: Socket.IO

docs.title: Security fixes release: 25 November 2026
docs.text:
This release has a security fix for the native HTTP server and for the native HTTP client. We recommend that you update. The server also has 10 more fixes, which the HTTP server tests of the Dart SDK found.

Key takeaways

  • Security fix: request smuggling. The server accepted a lone line feed in parts of a chunked request body. A proxy in front of the server could read the same bytes as two requests.
  • The same fix in the client. dox_http_client now refuses such bytes in a chunked answer.
  • The Dart SDK server tests now run against the server. They found 10 differences from dart:io, and each one is fixed.
  • Easy to update. Patch versions only. Run dart pub upgrade dox_http_native dox_http_client.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Package New version dox_http_native 3.2.5 dox_http_client 0.0.5

No change: all the other packages, the dox CLI and the app template.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Get the new versions of the 2 packages:

    dart pub upgrade dox_http_native dox_http_client

    This changes only these 2 packages. It also works when your app gets them through other Dox packages.

  2. Build or start the app again. The new native libraries download automatically.

There is no API change and no config change.

docs.title: Security fix: request smuggling
docs.text:
A request body with Transfer-Encoding: chunked comes in parts. Each part starts with a size line, and the body can end with trailer lines. Each line must end with .

The server accepted a lone in two places:

  • In a chunk extension, the text after ; in a size line. For example: 5;a b .
  • In a trailer line after the last part.

Some proxies end a line at a lone . Such a proxy and the server then see a different end of the body. An attacker can use this to hide a second request in the body of the first one. The proxy does not see this second request, so its rules do not apply to it. This attack is request smuggling. It is the same type as CVE-2025-55315 in ASP.NET Core and CVE-2026-19203 in Jetty.

Now the server answers 400 to a size line or a trailer that has a control byte, for example a lone , a lone or a NUL byte. A tab is permitted. A correct client never sends these bytes, so a normal request does not change.

Who is at risk: an app behind a proxy or a load balancer that reads chunked bodies with a lone as a line end. An app with no proxy in front of it is not at risk from this issue.

docs.title: The client
docs.text:
dox_http_client had the same issue when it read a chunked answer. Now each size line and each trailer line of an answer must end with \r\n, and an answer with a control byte in these lines fails with badResponse. Before, a server or a proxy could make the client read the rest of a body as the next answer on the same connection.

We found these issues in the security check that we do before each release of the HTTP packages. The fuzz tests now check the new rule too.

docs.title: Fixes from the Dart SDK tests
docs.text:
The Dart SDK has tests for its own HTTP server in dart:io. These tests now run against the native server in CI: 755 pass. The tests that do not apply to the native server are skipped. They found these differences, and each one is fixed:

  • A client that sent more than 64 pipelined requests, and then closed its send side, got answers for only the first 64.
  • A client that closed its connection in the middle of a request body kept the connection open until bodyTimeout.
  • requestedUri was wrong for a request line with an absolute URI, like GET http://example.com/ HTTP/1.1.
  • A size line that was empty, or that started with ;, was read as the last part of a chunked body. Now the request gets 400. This was also a request smuggling risk.
  • A handler that set a Date header made an answer with two Date headers.
  • response.headers.clear() did not reset chunkedTransferEncoding.
  • response.add with a value outside 0 to 255, like [256], sent other bytes. Now it throws an ArgumentError, as in dart:io.
  • The answer to a HEAD request had content-length: 0, not the length that the handler set.
  • NativeWebSocket.upgrade(protocol:) sent a protocol that the client did not offer. Now the request gets 500, as in dart:io.
  • When the stream of addStream failed before the head went out, the request got no answer. Now it gets 500.

Full list: the CHANGELOG of dox_http_native and of dox_http_client.

docs.title: What makes Dox fast
docs.text:
Dox is fast because your Dart code runs as a compiled binary, the network and database work happens in native code on the same thread, and most of the setup work is done once at build time or at start.

Your app is plain Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware and models. This post explains what Dox does around that code, one reason at a time. Each section links to the docs page with the details.

docs.title: A compiled binary
docs.text:
dox build compiles your app ahead of time (AOT) into a native binary. The code is machine code before the server starts. No compiler runs next to your app, and the server needs no Dart SDK.

dart run and dox serve use the JIT compiler. They are for development. They use much more memory and start slower. Always run the AOT binary in production.

See Deployment.

docs.title: A native HTTP server on the isolate's thread
docs.text:
Every Dox app runs on dox_http_native. It is written in Rust. It owns the sockets and parses HTTP. Your code still runs in Dart.

The server works in a loop on the isolate's own thread:

  1. Dart makes one call into the native code.
  2. The native code writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them to Dart as one batch.
  3. Dart runs your handlers and makes the next call with their answers.

Under load, no other thread is involved. So a request never waits for another thread to wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate is idle.

The server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer. Code written for dart:io keeps working.

See Native server.

docs.title: One isolate per CPU core
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core by default. Each isolate runs the whole app and its own server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

All isolates live in one process and share the compiled program. You do not need a process manager to use all cores.

See Isolate.

docs.title: Keep-alive and pipelining
docs.text:
A connection stays open for the next request (keep-alive). A client can also send many requests on one connection without waiting for each answer (pipelining).

There are limits, so one client can not fill the memory. At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer. At most 1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that connection until the answers go out.

See Native server: limits.

docs.title: Native database drivers
docs.text:
Postgres and MySQL use native drivers: dox_postgres_native and dox_mysql_native. Your models and queries stay in Dart. You do not change any config.

  • The database work runs on the thread of each isolate, like the HTTP server. There is no extra thread to hand a query to.
  • Many queries go down one connection at once (pipelining).
  • Dart sends many queries in one call. The results come back together.
  • All isolates share one pool. The pool size is for the whole process, so the database gets a known number of connections.

See Native Postgres driver, Native MySQL driver and the package READMEs on GitHub: dox-postgres-native and dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: Generated code, not reflection
docs.text:
Dox does not use dart:mirrors. Instead, build_runner with dox_builder writes plain Dart code for you:

  • the dependency injection container (lib/generated/container.g.dart),
  • the list of your Router classes, in the same file,
  • the DTO checks (a .dto.g.dart file next to each DTO),
  • the model classes.

The DTO rules, like @Email() or @Min(18), become typed Dart code at build time. They are not rule strings that are read on each request. This is also what makes the AOT build possible.

See Dependency injection and Validation.

docs.title: Work done once, not on each request
docs.text:
When an isolate starts, it does some work once:

  • It builds the pattern of each route.
  • It reads the parameter types of each controller.
  • It groups the routes by HTTP method.

On each request, Dox does less:

  • JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.
  • LogMiddleware collects log lines and writes them in one write every 20 ms (or every 64 KB). In a new project it is off in production.

See Performance: what Dox does for you and How Dox works.

docs.title: What Dox does not do
docs.text:
Some choices are left to you on purpose:

  • No VM flags. Dox never sets Dart VM flags for you. We tried a bigger young generation for a better p99. The change was inside the noise, so there is no flag to set. You can try your own with DART_VM_OPTIONS.
  • No gzip in Dart by default. gzip costs CPU on every response. A proxy like Caddy or nginx does it better. If you have no proxy, AppConfig(compress: true) turns it on, and the native server gzips on a helper thread.

See Performance: Dart VM flags and Performance: gzip.

docs.title: A few numbers
docs.text:
On 2 CPU cores, GET / with 256 connections, a full Dox app served 638,067 requests per second. A plain dart:io HttpServer, with no framework, served 129,796. In a small app that reads one row from Postgres (GET /db), Dox served 266,432 requests per second.

These numbers come from one machine and very small apps. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. Measure your own app. The Performance page has the full tables and how they were measured.
